articles.title: Marco Rubio In India: Can US Biz Diplomacy Ease Trump Tensions Over Tariffs, Russian Oil And Bring Trade Deal Closer? - Menafn
articles.summary: Marco Rubio In India: Can US Biz Diplomacy Ease Trump Tensions Over Tariffs, Russian Oil And Bring Trade Deal Closer?  Menafn
articles.full_text:
Rubio, who arrived in Mumbai on October 20 for a three-day visit, described India as a global“refining superpower” and said Washington would discuss opportunities for Reliance to process more Venezuelan crude at its Indian refineries.
He also indicated that the Indian conglomerate could explore producing oil in Venezuela.
The visit comes at a sensitive juncture in India-US relations, with trade disputes and tariff tensions persisting even as New Delhi continues to buy Russian crude to diversify its energy supplies and safeguard its energy security.
However, US President Donald Trump 's recent decision to waive potential sanctions-related tariffs on major buyers of Russian crude could remove one significant obstacle to a bilateral trade agreement, as per Reuters report.
Against this backdrop, Rubio's engagements with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai and Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani in Jamnagar underscore the importance Washington is placing on commercial and energy diplomacy alongside its broader strategic partnership with India.
India-US trade deal: 'Very, very close', says Rubio
Rubio struck an optimistic note on the long-pending India-US trade agreement, saying the negotiations were nearing completion, with only a few issues left to resolve.
“We're very, very close. I would say we're about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement,” Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday.
Following the meeting between Jaishankar and Rubio, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA ) said the two sides discussed a broad range of issues, including trade, defence, technology and energy security.
“They welcomed the progress made in negotiations on the India–U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA ) and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion,” the MEA said in a statement.
The ministers also exchanged views on regional and global developments, according to the ministry.
Why is Rubio visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar instead of Delhi?
One of the most striking aspects of Rubio's itinerary is its emphasis on India's and industrial centres rather than New Delhi, where high-level diplomatic engagements with visiting US officials would ordinarily be expected to take place.
Mumbai provides access to corporate leaders and financial institutions, while Jamnagar in Gujarat is home to Reliance Industries' twin refineries, which together form the world's largest single-location refining complex.
Also Read | India-US trade deal 'very close' to completion, Marco Rubio says
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has said that the visit would have a stronger focus, with Rubio scheduled to meet government officials in Mumbai and business representatives in Jamnagar.
Suresh K Goel, a former Indian diplomat, said the choice of locations raised questions about the nature of the visit and the agenda behind the engagements.
“If the Ministry of External Affairs prepared the programme, I do find it that this meeting was not scheduled earlier in Delhi and that he was going to Mumbai or to Jamnagar. Clearly, the agenda for the meeting was not official talks or anything,” Goel told LiveMint.
Why is Reliance Industries important to the US energy agenda?
Rubio's planned engagement with Reliance highlights the role India's refining capacity could play in Washington's efforts to expand markets for Venezuelan crude.
The US secretary of state said Washington would discuss encouraging Reliance to refine more Venezuelan oil at its Indian facilities and potentially explore oil production opportunities in Venezuela.
Reliance operates a massive refining complex in Jamnagar, giving it the capacity to process a wide range of crude grades. Its role could therefore be significant in any effort to expand the flow of Venezuelan oil to India.
For Washington, the discussions offer a potential commercial avenue for strengthening energy ties with India.
Rubio's visit is also expected to include a meeting with Reliance chairman Mukesh Ambani, bringing one of India's largest corporate groups into discussions that extend beyond conventional government-to-government diplomacy.
Russian oil, Trump's tariff threat and the road to a trade deal
Trump's administration had authorised the possibility of imposing tariffs of up to 100% on major importers of Russian oil, a measure that could have affected India, the world's second-largest buyer of Russian crude after China.
However, Trump recently waived potential tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian oil, removing one possible stumbling block in the trade negotiations with New Delhi, as per a Reuters report.
The move has also drawn criticism from US lawmakers who argue that Washington has been insufficiently tough on Moscow.
Why the strategic partnership still matters
Despite the strains over trade and Russian oil, India remains an important partner for the United States because of its economic potential, democratic institutions and cooperation across multiple strategic sectors, according to Goel.
Goel cautioned against allowing trade disputes or differences in diplomatic approach to overshadow the broader relationship.
“The relationship between India and the USA is very, very important in all respects. And therefore, the government, rather than becoming part of this temperament or trade effect kind of a thing, has to be mature in our dealing and try and see how we can actually conduct the relationship,” Goel told LiveMint.
He also emphasised India's significance as a democratic and economic partner for Washington in Asia.
“India continues to be important for the USA as an economic and democratic partner. After all, if you look at Asia, which is the other democracy which can compare in terms of relationship?” Goel said.

articles.full_text:
Robust crude oil flows out of the Middle East in recent weeks have started to pressure the key metric of strength for physical supply out of the region.
The premium of Oman crude over Dubai, the measure of Middle East’s market strength, has slumped this week to the lowest level since the end of July, to $4.22 per barrel, according to data by General Index cited by Bloomberg.
The Oman-Dubai crude differential had soared to as high as $65 in March when the Strait of Hormuz was at a virtual closure and no crude cargoes were moving out of the Middle East. The premium of Oman crude later slipped into a discount in the three weeks in the middle of June and early July, during which the U.S. and Iran were looking to negotiate a deal.
The differential blew out again in August and especially in September, when hostilities resumed.
But as the Middle Eastern producers accelerated shuttle-shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, flows have recovered in recent weeks.
The higher availability, especially of spot cargoes, led to the Oman crude premium to Dubai slumping from as high as $30 per barrel in the middle of September to just above $4 per barrel this week, per data by General Index.
Crude oil flows from the Middle East are recovering; many tanker-tracking services say they are even topping pre-war levels.
But the cost to move the crude out of the region is very high—freight rates have soared to record highs amid a shortage of tankers. The increased oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz, mostly thanks to ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, are tying up supertankers for weeks waiting for the transfers outside the Strait, limiting the availability of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) for other key global oil trade routes, such as the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia.

articles.title: Pakistan-Taliban conflict: How India could benefit from shifting regional dynamics - DW.com
articles.summary: Pakistan-Taliban conflict: How India could benefit from shifting regional dynamics  DW.com
articles.full_text:
Pakistan and Afghanistan right now are locked in a cycle of escalating tension. Repeated border clashes have strained ties between the two nations.
The current round of tensions began in February 2026, when Pakistan launched strikes into Afghanistan targeting Taliban militants. At one point in March, Pakistan's defense minister said the country was at "open war" with Afghanistan. Periodic bouts of violence have continued since then, with the latest Pakistani strikes targeting the Afghan Taliban's "terrorist hubs" reported earlier in October.
At the heart of the dispute is Pakistan's accusation that the Taliban authorities in Kabul allow the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group, to target Pakistan from Afghan territory. Kabul denies providing the group with sanctuary.
Where does India come into play?
As the two neighbors trade strikes, the escalating conflict "presents a significant diplomatic and strategic opportunity for India," Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, an Afghanistan expert and founder of the India-based Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.
D'Souza argues the confrontation has weakened Pakistan's traditional influence in Afghanistan and encouraged the Taliban to broaden its external relations.
"India can respond by expanding diplomatic engagement, humanitarian assistance, development projects and trade, while seeking assurances that Afghan territory will not be used by anti-India militant groups," she said.
However, D'Souza cautioned against interpreting the opening as a fundamental realignment.
"There is no ideological alignment between India and the Taliban," she said. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is likely to pursue a diversified foreign policy rather than align exclusively with New Delhi.
India also lacks the geographical advantages, economic leverage and security presence needed to replace Pakistan's influence, she notes. "The scenario of the Taliban becoming a strategic ally remains far-fetched."
Former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan Amar Sinha warned against viewing the conflict simply as an opportunity for New Delhi to gain at Pakistan's expense.
"The issues have very little to do with India," Sinha told DW, arguing that India was not seeking strategic advantage from the fighting. He also pointed to the consequences of Pakistan's military actions for Afghan civilians.
"Yet the rupture has made Kabul's search for alternative partners more pressing," he added.
For India, that creates an opening, but not necessarily a strategic alignment, Sinha notes. The Taliban can seek Indian assistance while maintaining relations with China, Russia, Iran and Gulf states, preserving its autonomy rather than exchanging dependence on Pakistan for dependence on India.
The cost of closer ties
Gautam Mukhopadhyaya, another former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan, sees the deterioration in relations between Pakistan and the Taliban as an opportunity for India to recover some of the strategic ground it lost when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
"The crisis has allowed strategic openings for India," Mukhopadhyaya told DW. He warned, however, that New Delhi's own treatment of Afghans could undermine its efforts to build a durable relationship.
He pointed to restrictions affecting Afghans seeking Indian visas for education, scholarships, work and medical treatment.
"For all practical purposes, India's security establishment treats Afghans as proxy Pakistanis and 'terrorists' by default," he said.
Former Afghan partners had been left "disappointed, even bitter," Mukhopadhyaya added. "A strategic relationship built on the sands of oppression is not a sound foundation."
Trade cannot overcome geography
India has restored air freight links between Kabul and Delhi and between Kabul and Amritsar in northwestern India in December 2025.
Bilateral trade between India and Afghanistan stood at about $908 million (€807 million) in the 2025-26 fiscal year, while trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan fell sharply amid repeated border closures.
On October 14, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi stressed the importance of relations with India during talks with Indian charge d'affaires Yatin Patel, signaling Kabul's interest in expanding economic cooperation.
But air freight is expensive, and India cannot easily replace Pakistan as a transit route.
New Delhi has sought to use Iran's Chabahar port to improve access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, but regional instability and complications surrounding Iran have constrained those ambitions.
D'Souza cautioned that "the ongoing conflict in Iran" limits India's ability to use Chabahar as a crucial trade and connectivity hub.
Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University specializing in Afghanistan and Eurasian connectivity, highlighted similar obstacles.
"In the last few decades, Islamabad has obstructed Kabul's efforts to gain access to the vast Indian market. However, political instability in Afghanistan and sanctions on Iran have undermined these efforts," Sachdeva told DW.
"Afghanistan's potential as a connector between regional markets remains considerable, but the infrastructure and political conditions needed to realize it are far from assured," he added.
Sachdeva also sees Russia and China as better positioned to shape Afghanistan's wider economic integration. Alternative routes may become more attractive to India, but they are not commercially viable overnight.
Islamabad's security fears
Pakistan has portrayed arch-rival India's growing engagement with the Taliban as a security threat. On October 7, Pakistani diplomat Muhammad Jawad Ajmal accused India at the United Nations of providing the Taliban with material and logistical support.
"Under the guise of humanitarian aid, they have been actively supporting the Taliban regime with material and logistical support for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan," Ajmal said.
The allegation reflects Islamabad's position and has not been established as fact.
Pakistan has accused India of supporting the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army, a militant organization.
India rejects accusations of backing militant activity, while the Taliban denies allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, offered a more nuanced assessment of Pakistan's position.
"India has stepped into a space and is trying to exert its influence and feed anti-Pakistan groups intelligence," she told DW.
Siddiqa added that Pakistan's establishment continues to view the crisis through "a singular security lens."
"Islamabad feels physically squeezed from both sides," she said, adding that closer Kabul-New Delhi ties could create "a dangerous two-front security trap" for Pakistan.
India may gain more room to operate in Afghanistan as ties between Kabul and Islamabad deteriorate. But the Taliban is unlikely to put all its eggs in New Delhi's basket.

Stellantis India aims to halve vehicle development time to 24 months and increase localisation as it prepares to launch 12 products across Citroen and Jeep under its FaSTLAne 2030 roadmap.
Stellantis India is targeting to halve vehicle development time and ramp up localisation for certain models as it prepares to launch 12 products across Citroen and Jeep brands under its FaSTLAne 2030 roadmap, MD and CEO Shailesh Hazela said.
"Globally, we announced that our ambition is to cut down our development time for bringing new products from 48 months to close to two years, which is around 24 months. That is what we are working on (for) our products, which we are going to launch," Hazela told PTI in an interview.
Stellantis has one of its software and technology centre in Bengaluru.
Also, Stellantis India has a long-standing partnership with Tata Motors Passenger Vehicle for manufacturing through a joint venture. Recently, they signed a definitive agreement to expand the scope of their partnership into advanced technology and product collaboration.
Both the companies plan to jointly develop vehicles for more than 50 global markets and manufacture them in India at Fiat India Automobiles Private Limited, the 50:50 joint venture between Tata Motors and Stellantis.
On localisation, Hazela said Citroen has localisation level in the range of 90-95 per cent, while Jeep brand's localisation stands at around 70-75 per cent.
"We are working on a foundation which is local engineering and local supply chain to get localisation of 90 per cent plus in our products here. That gives us flexibility to be in the pricing range that the market expects," he said.
Meanwhile, Stellantis India has announced an investment of ₹4,000 crore over the next three years as it prepares to launch 12 models, including seven new, across Citroen and Jeep brands. The investment will be mainly in products, localisation for customer experience.
Jeep brand currently has four models in India - Compass, Wrangler, Meridian and Grand Cherokee, while Citroen also has four models — C3, BasaltX, AircrossX, C5 Aircross.
Of the new products planned, Jeep brand will get four new models — one SUV each in B, C and D segments, along with a D segment pickup. Citroen will get three new models — one C segment SUV, D segment MPV and one A segment car.

- Copy link
At the RSS's 101st Foundation Day celebrations on Vijayadashami in Nagpur on 20 October, chief Mohan Bhagwat warned against foreign interference and attempts to change governments.
He raised concerns about ‘regime change’ and cited examples from countries such as Bangladesh, Nepal and France.
But what does regime change actually mean? Can protests really bring down a government, and could it happen in India?
Let us understand.
What did Mohan Bhagwat say about attempts to change India's government?
Mohan Bhagwat argued that powerful countries want to maintain their global dominance and may view India's growing influence as a challenge.
These were Bhagwat's allegations and assessments; his speech did not independently establish that a coordinated foreign-backed operation to change India's government was under way.
But Bhagwat did not make this warning in isolation. He pointed to political unrest in other countries to support his argument.
Why did Bhagwat compare India with France, Nepal, Bangladesh and Albania?
Bhagwat pointed to recent unrest in these four countries to support his warning that India could face attempts to destabilise its political system.
France
Student protests and wider civil unrest intensified amid anger over education, living costs and public services.
Albania
Protesters demanded Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation, and clashes with police and attacks on public buildings followed.
Bangladesh
Sheikh Hasina resigned as prime minister and left the country on 5 August, after more than 15 years in power.
Nepal
The unrest escalated, Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli resigned, and government buildings were attacked.
By citing these countries, Bhagwat suggested that India should be alert to a similar outcome.
How was France and Albania’s power topple different from India’s neighbours?
The main difference was the outcome.
Protests in Bangladesh and Nepal forced national leaders to leave office, while demonstrations in France and Albania had not toppled their national governments as of 20 October 2026.
However, this raises an important question:
What evidence would be needed to establish whether foreign powers are influencing protests or trying to change a government?
Why has the RSS raised concerns about foreign interference in India?
Several events over the past decade have shaped this debate.
‘Urban Naxal’ debate
2020-2021 Farmers' protests
2021 Toolkit controversy
The events above explain why the RSS is wary of foreign interference, but they raise a separate question.
Can foreign powers influence protests or attempts to change a government?
Yes, foreign powers can try to influence political movements through funding, misinformation and online propaganda. However, influencing a protest does not necessarily mean organising or controlling it.
In India's 2026 CJP protests, claims of support from Bangladesh's Jamaat-e-Islami circulated online. However, a purported support letter was found to be forged, and the party denied issuing it.

To understand how street movements can influence political outcomes, it is important to examine India's electoral history and the possibility of a shift in public opinion.

The Emergency offers a historical example.

articles.title: From Nepal, Sri Lanka to Bangladesh: How mass political protests left nations broken - Organiser Weekly
articles.summary: From Nepal, Sri Lanka to Bangladesh: How mass political protests left nations broken  Organiser Weekly
articles.full_text:
Mass protests are often presented as a means of bringing political change and demanding accountability. However, their economic consequences can extend well beyond the immediate political crisis. Prolonged agitation, disruption of public services and institutional instability can leave ordinary citizens struggling with lost income, rising prices and fewer employment opportunities.
Drawing on the experiences of Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal against treating political upheaval as a guaranteed path to democratic or economic improvement. The costs of instability are often borne by workers, small traders, daily-wage earners and middle-class households, even after the immediate political confrontation has ended.
Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal: Lessons from unrest
Sri Lanka’s Aragalaya movement culminated in the departure of President Gotabaya Rajapaksa in 2022, amid a severe economic crisis. Although the country has since made progress towards macroeconomic recovery under an International Monetary Fund-supported programme, the commentary points to continuing poverty and household financial pressures as reminders of the crisis’s long-term impact.
In Bangladesh, student-led protests over government job quotas in 2024 expanded into a wider anti-government movement that led to the fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government. Nalawade argues that the political transition did not automatically resolve the country’s economic difficulties, with inflation, industrial disruption and employment concerns continuing to affect ordinary people.
Nepal’s political turbulence has also be to put into question whether changes in government necessarily translate into lasting institutional or economic reform. Political leaders and influential groups can often adapt to changing circumstances, while citizens remain exposed to uncertainty and economic hardship.
Ordinary citizens bear the cost
There is vulnerability among people whose livelihoods depend on the uninterrupted movement of goods, functioning markets and stable employment. Prolonged road blockades can affect truck drivers and transport workers, while market closures and industrial disruptions can hurt small businesses, vendors and wage earners.
Economic instability can also reduce household purchasing power. When prices rise faster than wages, families face greater difficulty meeting basic expenses. For middle-class households, inflation can erode savings, while workers in vulnerable sectors may face reduced hours or job losses.
The political organisers and influential figures may be better placed to withstand these disruptions than the people who participate in, or are affected by, prolonged unrest.
India’s warning against prolonged disruption
Notably, India could face serious economic consequences if political mobilisation develops into sustained disruption of institutions, manufacturing centres and transport networks. It argues that political campaigns framed around constitutional protection and accountability should also be judged by their methods and their potential consequences for the wider public.
It is important to ask whether calls for nationwide agitation adequately account for the impact on small businesses, daily-wage workers, supply chains and investor confidence. It urges citizens to consider the economic consequences of prolonged unrest alongside the political demands being advanced.
The central argument is that democratic accountability and political reform should not be confused with disorder. Notably, India’s long-term strength depends on preserving institutional stability while allowing democratic debate and peaceful protest.

articles.title: How Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia are deepening defence ties - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: How Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia are deepening defence ties  Al JazeeraPak, Turkiye, Qatar, Indonesia sign def pact, experts say ‘Badr MoU’ won’t put New Delhi-Jakarta missile contracts in jeopardy  The Times of IndiaTurkey, Qatar, Pakistan, Indonesia sign defence cooperation accord, Ankara says  ReutersPakistan, Qatar, Turkiye and Indonesia sign 'Badr' defence cooperation pact  DawnPakistan, Turkiye, Qatar and Indonesia sign pact to bolster defe...
articles.full_text:
Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia signed a deal on Wednesday to deepen their defence industry cooperation, reflecting a broader effort by countries in the region to widen their network of security partners amid the prolonged US-Israel war with Iran.
The four countries signed the memorandum of understanding in Doha, building on existing military projects through joint production, technology transfers and more closely integrated supply chains.
The initiative comes as the failure of the United States and Iran to reach a concrete peace agreement pushes countries in the region to diversify their defence partnerships and look beyond what experts described as an overreliance on Washington for their security. But they stress that closer cooperation does not mean abandoning long-standing alliances. Instead, the ambition is to gain greater control over their own security while strengthening pre-existing partnerships.
Arda Mevlutoglu, a defence industry analyst and managing director of Mergen Analytical Strategies, told Al Jazeera that the implications could extend well beyond the four participants.
“We may be witnessing the emergence of an interconnected network of defence and security arrangements extending from the Gulf to South and Southeast Asia, rather than a single formal alliance,” he said.
What would the agreement do?
In a statement, the Qatari Defence Ministry said the “Badr” Memorandum of Understanding “aims to foster cooperation in the field of defence manufacturing, enhance defence capabilities among the four countries, and promote collaboration in technical defence training, as well as in research and development areas, thereby contributing to the creation of solutions and industries worthy of the evolution of modern defences”.
Experts say that under the agreement, each country will bring its own resources or set of skills to the table. “Turkiye contributes technological expertise, systems integration and a mature defence industry; Pakistan and Indonesia offer manufacturing capacity, skilled workforces and sizeable domestic markets; and Qatar provides investment potential and demand,” said Mevlutoglu.
Together, the four nations could “establish integrated supply chains, allowing these countries to jointly develop, manufacture and sustain defence systems”, he told Al Jazeera.
Such arrangements could give buyers a larger role in producing and supporting their own equipment, while providing manufacturers with longer-term orders and investment. Albert Vidal, a research associate at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that Pakistan and Indonesia were both willing to purchase Turkish weapons and locate part of their production at home.
This could bring down costs for Turkish companies and bring jobs to Pakistan and Indonesia, while Qatar brings “financial depth”, he said.
Building on existing partnerships
Turkiye, home to one of the world’s most advanced defence sectors, already has military manufacturing ties with Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia separately. Qatar and Turkiye, for instance, signed a bilateral defence industry memorandum in October 2025.
But Vidal says that the new agreement, bringing together all four nations, points to a strategic calculation alongside an industrial one. Closer relationships could give more countries a stake in each other’s security. He pointed to Qatar’s investment in the Turkish defence industry over more than a decade and Ankara’s deployment of forces to Doha during the 2017 diplomatic crisis.
Pakistan’s existing naval manufacturing project with Turkiye, meanwhile, shows how weapons purchases can support domestic manufacturing. Of the four ships announced under the project, two are to be built in Istanbul and two at Karachi Shipyard.
Indonesia and Turkiye, meanwhile, are jointly building a tank.
“The rationale is to streamline these distinct defence export and joint production agreements under a more structured and resilient networked hub, rather than reinvent the wheel with each new defence agreement,” Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera.
Less dependence on Washington?
The US-Israeli war with Iran and recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have heightened regional security concerns, analysts say, while reported US weapons shortages may be adding urgency to efforts to strengthen pre-existing partners and bolster domestic arms-building capacity.
“Diversification is a major driver, particularly as recent conflicts have exposed vulnerabilities associated with dependence on foreign suppliers, technology restrictions and supply chain disruptions,” Mevlutoglu said.
But he cautioned against interpreting the memorandum as a break with Washington. “Qatar is unlikely to abandon its strategic relationship with Washington, while Turkiye seeks greater technological independence within NATO, not autonomy from it,” he said.
According to Bader Mousa Al-Saif, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme and an assistant professor at Kuwait University, the initiative reflects Gulf countries increasingly looking towards the Global South and fellow Muslim countries.
It also complements a separate effort to formalise military cooperation across the region, analysts say. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, establishing a mutual defence commitment. Ankara submitted the agreement to parliament for ratification on Wednesday, although deploying Turkish troops abroad would require separate parliamentary approval.
The Doha memorandum concerns industrial cooperation rather than a mutual defence pledge, but Mevlutoglu sees a connection between the two initiatives. “While Mecca focuses on collective deterrence and military cooperation, Doha could provide the industrial and technological foundations for such partnerships,” he said.

articles.title: Who is the next Republican nominee for US President? JD Vance expects 2028 endorsement; Trump says 'no' - The Times of India
articles.summary: Who is the next Republican nominee for US President? JD Vance expects 2028 endorsement; Trump says 'no'  The Times of IndiaJD Vance’s 2028 Ambitions Face an Early Test in Midterms  Bloomberg.comVance reveals the Trump dilemma that could complicate his 2028 White House ambitions  Fox NewsVance hints that he may not run for president in 2028  WSMHVance’s Delicate 2028 Dance  RealClearPolicy
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump has declined to endorse Vice President JD Vance as his successor in the 2028 presidential election, despite Vance saying he expects to receive Trump's backing if he decides to run.
Asked whether he viewed Vance as his successor and the Republican nominee for 2028, Trump replied, “No.” He then described Vance as “a very capable” person, adding that there were several capable people who could potentially succeed him.
Trump's remarks came after Vance said he believed the president would endorse him if he entered the race, while also acknowledging that he had not discussed the possibility with Trump.
What Trump said about Vance
During the exchange, Trump was asked directly whether he saw Vance as his political successor and the Republican Party's nominee in 2028. His response was an unambiguous “No”, followed by a more favourable assessment of the vice president's abilities.
“But he is a very capable, You know you have a lot of capable people,” Trump said.
The remarks stop short of ruling out Vance as a potential successor, but Trump did not commit to backing him for the Republican nomination.
Vance expects Trump's backing but leaves room for a contest
Vance, meanwhile, said he believed Trump would endorse him if he decided to contest the 2028 presidential election.
“Look, I think if I run, the president will endorse me,” Vance said during an interview.
Asked whether Trump would endorse him immediately after an announcement, Vance said he expected to receive the president's support but acknowledged that he had not discussed the matter with him.
“I would think so, but I don't know, man. I haven't talked to him about it,” Vance said.
He also suggested that Trump's endorsement would not necessarily need to determine the outcome of the Republican nomination contest.

New Delhi, Oct 21 (IANS) The growth rate of India’s core sector industries surged to a 30-month high of 7.9 per cent in September, compared to the same month of the previous year, driven by the strong performance of the iron ore, electricity, coal refinery products, cement, and steel sectors, according to figures released by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Wednesday.
The production of iron ore surged by as much as 18.4 per cent in September. Owing to intensive use of iron ore in the production process and its contribution to industrial development, it has been included in the list of core industries as a new item in the revised series of the index of core industries (ICI). Accordingly, the number of core industries has increased from eight to nine in the new series, which kicked in for the first time last month.
Electricity generation grew by 11.4 per cent during September while coal production went up by 10.7 per cent. The output of refinery products increased by 10.7 per cent during the month as demand for petroleum goods rose due to the higher level of economic activity.
The cement sector clocked a robust growth of 10.3 per cent while steel production was up 4.9 per cent during the month as demand stayed buoyant due to large government investments in big-ticket infrastructure projects such as highways, ports and railways.
However, fertilisers, natural gas, and crude oil witnessed negative growth in September.
The final index for the month of August 2026 has been revised from 119.2 to 120.4. Accordingly, the year-on-year growth rate has been revised from 4.8 per cent to 5.9 per cent.
Cumulative growth rate of the index of core industries during April-September 2026 now works out to 5.1 per cent compared to 2.5 per cent in the corresponding period of the previous year, reflecting the acceleration in the growth of the infrastructure industries.
The Office of Economic Adviser, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) has released the revised series of Index of Core Industries (ICI) with Base Year 2022-23 for the first time in July this year. Washington — President Donald Trump said the United States and India are approaching a bilateral trade agreement, suggesting that a deal could be finalized soon while indicating that its terms would differ significantly from previous trade arrangements.
Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office alongside Vice President JD Vance, Trump expressed confidence that negotiations with New Delhi were nearing a conclusion.
“They want to make a deal. We’re going to make a deal pretty close,” Trump said when asked about the status of trade discussions between the two countries.
“Yeah, that’s going to be a much different kind of deal than we’ve made,” he added.
The president did not elaborate on how the proposed agreement would differ from previous trade deals or provide a timeline for its completion.
His remarks came as Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited India for discussions with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, highlighting continued diplomatic engagement between Washington and New Delhi.
The comments add to indications of progress in negotiations that have drawn considerable attention from businesses, exporters and investors in both countries.
India and the United States have been working toward a bilateral trade agreement designed to expand market access, reduce trade barriers and address longstanding differences involving tariffs, agricultural products, industrial goods and regulatory requirements.
The negotiations have taken on greater importance under Trump’s second administration, which has placed tariffs and reciprocal trade arrangements at the center of its economic policy.
The administration has maintained that major trading partners should provide American businesses with greater access to their domestic markets while reducing restrictions on U.S. exports.
For India, the outcome could have significant implications for industries such as pharmaceuticals, textiles, engineering goods, electronics and information technology services.
American businesses are also seeking expanded opportunities in India’s growing consumer market and manufacturing sector.
Despite expressing optimism, Trump did not indicate whether negotiators had resolved disagreements over specific products, tariff reductions or market-access provisions.
He also did not announce any new investment commitments, trade concessions or implementation schedule.
The president made his comments during an Oval Office event focused primarily on combating fraud involving federal government programs.
Trump and Vance announced incentives intended to encourage individuals to report suspected misuse of taxpayer funds while discussing broader administration economic priorities.
During the event, Trump also addressed U.S. trade deficits with major partners, including Canada, Mexico and the European Union, arguing that his administration’s policies were reshaping longstanding commercial relationships.
He credited his tariff strategy with encouraging investment in American manufacturing and industrial facilities and presented the administration’s trade policies as part of its efforts to expand domestic production and employment.
Although Trump did not specifically address Indian tariffs or the bilateral trade balance during the exchange, his remarks about India came amid his broader push for new trade arrangements with major economic partners.
Washington and New Delhi have held months of discussions over a potential agreement, with trade and investment remaining central components of the broader bilateral relationship.
The two countries also maintain extensive cooperation in defense, technology, energy security and manufacturing.
The United States is among India’s largest trading partners, with commercial ties spanning goods, services, technology, pharmaceuticals and financial services.
While Trump’s latest comments signal continued momentum in the negotiations, the final terms and timing of a trade agreement remain unannounced. (Source: IANS)

articles.title: Attracting high-tech investment: Lessons from India for Vietnam - Vietnam.vn

articles.full_text:
Backed by billions of dollars in subsidies, India's high-tech manufacturing sector is steadily integrating into global supply chains, but still faces challenges related to added value and investment efficiency.
This experience highlights the requirements for Vietnam in implementing Resolution 57: attracting investment must go hand in hand with enhancing endogenous technological capacity and mastering high-value-added stages.
Optimists argue that Apple's move to shift some iPhone production to India helps the country reduce its dependence on China and improve its position in the global supply chain. Currently, about a quarter of iPhones are manufactured in factories near Chennai, providing jobs for tens of thousands of workers.
However, skeptics argue that much of the activity remains focused on final assembly, which creates little added value. Nevertheless, Indian factories have begun taking on more stages, from assembling components onto circuit boards to manufacturing motherboards.
The core question is whether these advances are commensurate with the state subsidies. If competitiveness cannot be maintained without budgetary support, the gains of India's manufacturing sector risk reversing.

Smartphones use many high-value components such as circuit boards, camera modules, and screens. To truly improve its position in the production chain, the export value of finished phones needs to increase faster than the import of input components.
However, the evaluation is not simple because many imported components are also used in electric vehicles , solar panels, and other equipment.
In 2023, former Reserve Bank of India Governor Raghuram Rajan and two colleagues developed three scenarios, assuming that 40%, 60%, or 80% of imported components in the multipurpose category were used in mobile phones. In all three cases, India's mobile phone trade balance remained in deficit. The research team argued that the increase in finished phone exports was not enough to demonstrate that the country's manufacturing capacity had reached a breakthrough.
Newer analysis shows that the trade balance remains in deficit, but the gap between component imports and phone exports has narrowed. This indicates progress in domestic manufacturing, although it is not yet possible to say that India has mastered the majority of the product's value.
Value added remains limited.
You may also like
Indian suppliers have expanded into more complex processes, but the lack of mastery in the production of memory chips, processors, lenses, displays, and batteries still limits the ability to create domestic value.
With the iPhone 14, India narrowed the production gap with China to just two months, up from six to nine months previously. The iPhone 15 was the first model Apple manufactured in India to be ready for the global launch from day one.
Suppliers, including Foxconn, have also shifted from importing complete circuit boards to assembling components directly in India. Motherboard manufacturing alone is expected to improve the trade balance by $2.1 billion in the 2025-2026 fiscal year.
However, the outlook remains uncertain. Strong demand for memory chips from data centers is driving up the price of semiconductors used in phones. Meanwhile, demand for phones in the Indian market is declining, especially in the low-cost segment. This could reduce component imports, but weaker global smartphone sales also risk impacting exports.
Subsidies are putting increasing pressure on the budget.
Five years ago, India implemented a subsidy program equivalent to 4-6% of the finished phone bill value to offset infrastructure disadvantages and production costs. As chip prices rise due to demand from the artificial intelligence (AI) sector, the budget may have to bear additional support costs.
With a subsidy rate of 4%, for every additional $1 billion in the bill value solely due to rising chip prices, the budget would have to spend an extra $40 million. Thus, even if production doesn't increase proportionally, the cost of subsidies could still balloon.
To move further into the supply chain, the Indian government has allocated an additional $13.4 billion to develop the domestic semiconductor industry. However, the $10 billion subsidy introduced five years ago has mainly helped establish overseas chip packaging facilities, failing to create advanced chip manufacturing capabilities.
Advanced chip manufacturing requires cutting-edge technology, significant capital investment, and the ability to accept long periods without profitability. India still faces challenges in all three areas. Even Tata Group, a key Apple partner in the country and the company behind India's only semiconductor manufacturing plant project, is facing disputes over control and concerns related to the scale of investment in the electronics sector.
International experience shows that moving up to higher-tech stages is not easy. Malaysia developed chip packaging and circuit board assembly operations from the 1970s, but its progress up the value chain stalled after the country reached upper-middle income status in 1992. Meanwhile, South Korea and Taiwan (China) leveraged the semiconductor industry to rise to the ranks of wealthy economies.
It's not easy to copy the Chinese model.
India can hardly rely solely on billions of dollars in investment to quickly catch up with the world's leading high-tech manufacturing hubs. Instead, it needs to develop its design and engineering capabilities while allocating resources to healthcare, education, climate change response, and labor-intensive industries such as textiles, footwear, and toys.
You may also like
The Chinese model is particularly difficult to replicate. Apple's success in the country is linked to Foxconn's ability to coordinate with local authorities to rapidly build large-scale factory complexes. This combination of deployment speed, production scale, and risk tolerance is an advantage that India will find difficult to replicate.
Apple may be able to help India improve its manufacturing capabilities and become more deeply involved in the global supply chain, but that doesn't mean the country will become the next factory of the world. Continuing to increase subsidies in the hope of replicating the Chinese model could lead to ever-increasing costs without necessarily delivering commensurate benefits.
From attracting investment to mastering technology: Lessons for Vietnam
Drawing lessons from India's experience, Vietnam can develop high-tech industries in line with the spirit of Resolution 57-NQ/TW dated December 22, 2024, of the Politburo on breakthroughs in national science, technology, innovation, and digital transformation. Investment incentives may attract large corporations, but they cannot replace endogenous technological capabilities and the ability to master high value-added processes.
Therefore, support policies need to be linked to tangible results such as technology transfer, development of supporting industries, training of high-quality human resources, and enhancement of research, design, and manufacturing capabilities. Regular evaluation of budget utilization efficiency is also essential to limit prolonged reliance on incentives without building sustainable competitiveness.
More importantly, Vietnam needs to focus on investing in research and development, digital infrastructure, education, and linkages between businesses and research institutions. This is the foundation for science, technology, and innovation to truly become a driving force for productivity enhancement, helping domestic businesses move up to higher value-added stages in the global supply chain, instead of primarily relying on processing and assembly.

Visa refusal rates for the UK have remained high for the last three quarters with no indication of dropping. Behind the surge in refusals is a clear pattern of seven countries generating more than 70% of visa refusals, namely: India, Nigeria, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Ghana and Sri Lanka.
These seven countries represent the volume application markets where visa refusal rates are above the government’s own 5% threshold classified as high risk. There are other markets with visa refusal rates above 50% such as Kenya and Iran, but with much lower application levels. 
Refusal rates for different nationalities have spiked at different points over the last three quarters, however the 12-month rolling average has shown a consistent rise. There has been no rebalancing of rates over time despite the fact universities have increased their compliance activity. 
In comparison with lower refusal rates for other countries, there seems to be an explicit message from the government to universities attracting international students: recruit from these markets at your own risk. 
Some universities have taken heed, stopping recruitment entirely from entire countries including Pakistan, Bangladesh, Ghana and Sri Lanka in recent months.
The inclusion of India, the UK’s largest student source market, in the list of high risk countries will be of concern to the sector. The country’s average visa refusal rate has now crept to 8% across the last three quarters, above the target 5% threshold outlined in the new BCA metrics. 
The idea of stopping recruitment from India is unfathomable, but recruitment clearly comes with some significant risk now, linked to certain regions within the country. As a shared, sector-wide volume market, this introduces jeopardy even for Russell Group institutions as explained in our mission group analysis.
It is also notable that In Q2 2026, visa refusals for Nigerian and Ghanan nationals rose sharply, reaching their highest levels in the past 12- months. University sources told The PIE, the sharp increase can be linked to a backlog of applications that were awaiting a decision for more than three months being refused at the same time, although we are unable to verify this claim.

articles.title: India-US trade deal: Rubio says pact is ‘incredibly close’, ‘matter of weeks, not months’ - Upstox
articles.summary: India-US trade deal: Rubio says pact is ‘incredibly close’, ‘matter of weeks, not months’  Upstox
articles.full_text:
Business News
SUMMARY
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio expects an announcement within weeks, potentially followed by a signing by the two countries’ leaders.
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar shakes hands with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the presence of Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, right, and US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, left, during a bilateral meeting, in Mumbai.
The United States and India are close to finalising a trade agreement, with only a few technical details left to resolve, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday.
"We're about as close as you can be without having an executed agreement," Rubio said at a press conference after meeting External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai.
"I think there's a small number of items left to wrap up. So I think that will happen shortly - we're hoping, which it should -- and hopefully have some good news to announce fairly soon." he said. “And perhaps the leaders can sign it thereafter.”
In an interview with News18, Rubio said the agreement was expected within weeks rather than months, but stressed that both sides needed to settle every detail before announcing it.
"It's incredibly close. I think we're down to some technical details that have to be worked out. Technical details matter because there has to be agreement. Both sides have to agree that the language means the same thing. So it’s down to that level," Rubio said.
Rubio said he was not directly negotiating the pact, which is being handled by the US Trade Representative, but had been closely involved in following the discussions.
"But I know – and have been very involved in watching it happen – that it is something we anticipate seeing in a matter of weeks, not months," he added.
The two countries announced in February the finalisation of a framework for the first phase of a bilateral trade agreement. Subsequent changes in the US tariff regime led to further negotiations.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said last month that the trade pact was "done and dusted", but its execution was awaiting a competitive advantage for Indian exporters over rivals in other countries.
"We have to find the right comparable competitive advantage over our competitors, so that we can quickly execute the agreement," Goyal said ahead of his visit to the United States.
India competes with countries including Bangladesh, Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Sri Lanka in several US markets.
Preferential tariffs for Indian goods compared with those of these competitors would improve the price competitiveness of Indian exporters.
Following his meeting with Rubio, Jaishankar said on social media that the two had "shared views on further advancement of our ties, focusing on trade, energy, technology, defence and people-to-people ties".
The US State Department said the two diplomats also discussed regional and global issues, including developments in West Asia.
"The secretary reiterated that increased energy trade with the United States can play a transformative role in diversifying India's supply chains while meeting its sizable consumer demand," the department said.
Rubio also commended progress in bilateral defence and civil nuclear cooperation and advocated increased purchases of US technologies and systems, it added.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor described the discussions as productive, saying the two sides were working to deepen cooperation in defence, energy, emerging technologies and trade.
Rubio also addressed questions about India's purchases of Russian oil and its efforts to reduce dependence on Russian energy supplies, saying New Delhi's push to diversify its energy sources was a sensible approach.
"I think they've made substantial progress in that regard, and we're happy to see that. But in the end, it's not just about Russian oil; it's about their desire to diversify, and obviously we think we can be a source of some of their energy inputs."
"Obviously, we've discussed Venezuela and other countries, and I think it's in our interest to have a strong ally with a diverse energy portfolio," he said.
Rubio said India had significant oil-refining capabilities and that some Indian companies already held oil concessions in Venezuela.
"I'm not claiming to you that Venezuela alone can fill the hole that could be caused by some of the things that are happening around the world, but I think over time, it most certainly can," he said.
Rubio visited Reliance Industries' refinery in Jamnagar on Wednesday, saying energy was closely linked to national security and economic stability.
"Countries fight wars over energy, economies collapse over lack of energy," he said.
Before his talks with Jaishankar, Rubio visited the Taj memorial in Mumbai and laid a wreath in honour of victims of the November 2008 attacks, which killed 166 people, including six American citizens.
Rubio said the purpose of a trade agreement was to secure better terms than those currently available, while ensuring that the arrangement remained beneficial to both countries over the long term.
"For a trade deal with India, or any country for that matter, to be sustainable in the long term, it has to be an agreement that is good for both sides," he said.
He said differences were inevitable because countries would defend their respective national interests, but close relations could help bridge those differences.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman recently said the negotiations were continuing, while acknowledging that both sides might have reached a stage where further concessions would be difficult.
"The agreement negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult," she said at the Munich Leaders Meeting.
"But maybe if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it," she added.
The United States is India's largest export destination and second-largest trading partner. India's goods exports to the United States were valued at about $87.3 billion in 2025, while bilateral goods trade stood at nearly $141 billion.

NEW DELHI: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India on Tuesday for talks on the ongoing negotiations over trade tariffs, defense cooperation and energy security.
Starting his trip in India’s financial capital, Mumbai, Rubio was received by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and will hold meetings with business leaders.
“We shared views on further advancement of our ties, focusing on trade, energy, technology, defense and people-to-people ties,” Jaishankar said after the meeting.
The visit comes days after US President Donald Trump waived potential tariffs on India for its Russian oil purchases, as the American administration pursues a bilateral trade agreement.
Rubio told reporters in Mumbai that the US was “very close” to finalizing the deal.
“I would say we’re about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement. I think there’s a small number of items left to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly,” he said.
On his two-day trip, he is scheduled to visit on Wednesday the Reliance Industries crude oil refining complex in Jamnagar, the world’s largest such facility, which belongs to Mukesh Ambani, India’s second-richest man.
“India is a refining superpower. They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They’ve done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, it’s something they can do,” Rubio said, asked if he would encourage Reliance to enter production in Venezuela, whose vast petroleum reserves have been managed by the US administration since it ousted the South American nation’s former President Nicolas Maduro in January.
“I think what India has expressed repeatedly is its desire to diversify its energy portfolio, which is a smart thing to do ... We’ve discussed Venezuela and other countries, and I think it’s in our interest to have strong allies with diverse energy portfolios.”
It is Rubio’s second India trip this year and follows his visit to Uzbekistan, where he met Central Asian business leaders.
According to Anil Raman, research fellow at the Takshashila Institution, the Asia tour, including India, is focused on economic and commercial negotiations ahead of the US midterm elections next month, where increasing grocery and fuel prices due to Trump’s war with Iran are among Americans’ top concerns.
“He’s coming along with 200-odd businessmen,” Raman said. “The economy is the main thing on the agenda in the midterm elections, so they have to show that they’re making an effort to sort of resolve these things. I think that’s a reason for Marco Rubio’s visit at this particular time.”

articles.title: India, China Maintain Dialogue to Manage Tensions, but Unresolved Border and Strategic Disputes Block Reset: Report - Defence.in
articles.summary: India, China Maintain Dialogue to Manage Tensions, but Unresolved Border and Strategic Disputes Block Reset: Report  Defence.in
articles.full_text:
The unresolved border dispute remains a central security concern and the principal obstacle in India-China relations which are still short of their pre-2020 status quo despite Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi last month for the BRICS summit prompting speculation that both countries are moving toward a reset, a report has highlighted.
India has sought to stabilise ties and manage differences with China since the 2020 Galwan clashes with the efforts gaining momentum due to US President Donald Trump’s increasingly hostile policies toward India and much of Asia, a report in The Diplomat highlighted.
However, Xi’s New Delhi visit for the BRICS Summit in September and the bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi should not be mistaken for an alignment of interests, the report cautioned.
“The resumption of high-level dialogue, leadership meetings, and direct connectivity are important developments. Another Galwan-like border confrontation would carry heavy domestic costs and could be difficult to recover from. Preventing a recurrence of such violence is a priority. But this does not require India to reconsider its position on the underlying differences,” wrote Sana Hashmi, a fellow at the Taiwan-Asia Exchange Foundation.
“It is also important to note that India never abandoned dialogue with China after Galwan. Keeping communication channel open has remained part of its approach, even as tensions persisted along the border. The latest meetings continue that policy; they do not demonstrate that the relationship or India’s approach to it has fundamentally changed,” Hashmi mentioned.
The report mentioned that China’s recent statement that it does not recognise the Union Territory of Ladakh, underlines the depth of the disagreement.
“There is little basis for expecting a reset while the two sides remain so far apart on territorial issues. Nor is the border the only source of friction. China’s relationship with Pakistan and the persistent trade imbalance remain contentious issues, too. There is little evidence of progress on any of these fundamental differences,” it added.
The Diplomat report stated that the Galwan clashes changed India’s view of and threat perception from China and raised serious questions about the viability of the existing arrangements in ensuring peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).
“High-level meetings can help manage tensions for the time being, but they cannot substitute for progress on the ground. India is also unlikely to return to its previous position on the One China policy without some reference to, or assurance regarding, a corresponding One India policy from Beijing. Such an assurance appears unlikely in the foreseeable future,” Hashmi opined.
“Just a couple of years ago, a meeting between Xi and Modi on Indian soil seemed difficult to imagine. That is one of the reasons why their meeting drew so much attention. But it has not changed the scope or nature of the issues dividing the two countries. For now, both sides are trying to prevent another crisis while their core disagreements remain unresolved. Until those differences are addressed, dialogue may keep the relationship from deteriorating further, but it will not put China-India ties on the path to a reset,” the expert added.
During their meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12, PM Modi had reiterated to Xi Jinping that India and China should show sensitivity to each other’s core concerns and be guided by mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity.
Both leaders had emphasised that “differences should not become disputes” and reaffirmed that the two countries should take a strategic and long term perspective of their ties.
“The two leaders welcomed the steady progress in India-China bilateral relations since their last meeting in Tianjin in August 2025. They reaffirmed that both countries should take a strategic and long term perspective of their ties. Differences should not become disputes. Prime Minister highlighted that both sides must be guided by three mutuals- mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest,” read a statement issued by the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) after the meeting.

articles.title: Marco Rubio Arrives in India: Jaishankar Meeting to Focus on Trade Deal, Defence and Russian Oil - The Sunday Guardian
articles.summary: Marco Rubio Arrives in India: Jaishankar Meeting to Focus on Trade Deal, Defence and Russian Oil  The Sunday Guardian
articles.full_text:
India and the United States are expected to discuss ways to strengthen cooperation in defence, security, technology, energy and critical minerals when External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar meets US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Mumbai on Tuesday. The meeting comes at a time when bilateral relations are facing challenges over trade, tariffs, energy supplies and other policy differences.
Rubio is scheduled to arrive in Mumbai on Tuesday afternoon with a large business delegation following his visit to Uzbekistan. This will be his second visit to India since May, when he held bilateral talks with Jaishankar and participated in a Quad foreign ministers’ meeting in New Delhi.
His visit also comes days after US President Donald Trump waived provisions of the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA), which authorised punitive tariffs against countries purchasing Russian oil. The move is significant for India, given its energy ties with Russia and concerns about the potential impact of US sanctions on bilateral relations and global energy markets.
According to people familiar with the matter, Jaishankar and Rubio are expected to focus on sustaining engagement between the two countries and advancing cooperation across several strategic and economic sectors.
India-US Talks to Focus on Trade, Energy and Critical Minerals
A key priority of the meeting will be to maintain momentum in India-US relations despite the differences that have emerged over the past year. Discussions are expected to cover trade, energy, technology, defence and security, along with cooperation on critical minerals.
India has already communicated its concerns to the US administration regarding the SRIA provisions and their possible consequences for bilateral ties and international energy markets.
The two sides are also expected to explore ways to strengthen economic cooperation and identify areas where progress can be made despite continuing disagreements. The talks come as negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement appear to have slowed, with officials on both sides seeking a mutually acceptable way forward.
The discussions could provide an opportunity for both governments to assess outstanding issues and identify practical steps to improve cooperation.
Jaishankar and Rubio to Discuss Ukraine and West Asia Conflicts
Regional and international developments are also expected to feature prominently in the discussions. Jaishankar and Rubio are likely to review the conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia and examine their impact on global food, fuel and fertiliser supplies.
India has proposed a ceasefire framework for the Russia-Ukraine conflict aimed at protecting essential supply routes. The proposal seeks to maintain the movement of energy and food supplies while preventing attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
Disruptions caused by these conflicts have raised concerns about energy security, food availability and supply chains. Both countries are expected to discuss these challenges and explore areas where their positions and interests could align.
India-US Leaders May Meet at ASEAN and G20 Summits
The possibility of meetings between senior leaders from India and the US on the sidelines of upcoming multilateral events is also expected to be discussed.
These engagements could include the ASEAN Summit in Manila next month and the G20 Summit in Florida, United States. Such meetings may provide opportunities to address outstanding bilateral issues and maintain high-level communication between the two governments.
Jaishankar is also scheduled to attend a celebration marking the 250th anniversary of American independence as the guest of honour.
These diplomatic engagements come at a time when both countries are seeking to preserve their strategic partnership despite disagreements over trade, tariffs and other policy matters.
Trade and Tariff Disputes Put Bilateral Relations Under Pressure
India-US relations have experienced significant strains over the past year, largely because of the Trump administration’s trade and tariff policies. Restrictions affecting Indian professionals and Washington’s growing engagement with Pakistan have also contributed to tensions.
Negotiations on a bilateral trade agreement have faced difficulties, with officials from both countries continuing to look for a mutually acceptable arrangement.
The proposed agreement is an important part of the broader economic relationship between the two countries. However, differences over trade terms and tariff measures have complicated efforts to reach a deal.
The Jaishankar-Rubio meeting is expected to provide an opportunity to review these challenges and explore ways to prevent disagreements from affecting cooperation in other strategic areas.
Rubio to Visit Reliance Industries’ Jamnagar Refinery
Rubio’s India itinerary includes a visit to Reliance Industries’ refinery in Jamnagar, Gujarat, on October 21. The facility is a major processor of Russian oil, making the visit particularly relevant amid discussions about sanctions, energy supplies and trade relations.
Reliance Industries is also investing in a large refinery project in Texas, described in the report as the first new project of its kind in the United States in five decades. The company is additionally a significant purchaser of Venezuelan oil, whose sales are controlled by the Trump administration.
The visit could bring attention to the links between energy trade, private-sector investment and the broader economic relationship between India and the US.
With energy security remaining a major concern for both countries, the discussions take place against the backdrop of changing global oil flows and Washington’s approach to sanctions on Russian and Venezuelan energy.
Rubio Acknowledges India’s Dependence on Russian Oil
Ahead of his visit, Rubio recognised India’s continued reliance on Russian energy, even as the country has diversified its sources of oil imports.
Commenting on the challenges of changing energy suppliers, he said that “it’s hard to pivot” on oil suppliers.
Rubio also indicated that Trump intended to use the 60-day waiver period under the SRIA to assess the broader economic consequences of sanctions and tariffs.
The remarks suggest that Washington is examining how its restrictions affect global markets and countries that depend on Russian oil. For India, the issue remains important because changes in energy supplies and trade restrictions could influence costs, supply security and bilateral relations.
US Ambassador’s Remarks Spark Political Debate in India
Before Rubio’s arrival, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor’s comments about Jaishankar being expected to travel to Mumbai to meet the secretary of state drew criticism from opposition parties.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs responded by stating that hosting foreign dignitaries outside New Delhi has been an established practice over the past decade.
The exchange brought additional attention to the arrangements surrounding Rubio’s visit, although the main focus of the meeting is expected to remain on bilateral cooperation and international developments.
Jaishankar to Hold Separate Talks With UAE Foreign Minister
Before meeting Rubio, Jaishankar is scheduled to host United Arab Emirates Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan for dinner on Monday evening.
The two leaders are expected to review bilateral cooperation and discuss ways to advance initiatives in energy, trade, investment and defence.
They will also exchange views on the evolving situation in West Asia, where continuing conflicts have raised concerns about regional stability and the security of vital energy and commercial routes.
The meeting reflects India’s efforts to maintain engagement with key regional partners while addressing economic and security challenges.
India-US Relations Face a Crucial Diplomatic Test
Rubio’s visit comes at a sensitive time for India-US relations, with both countries seeking to strengthen cooperation while managing disagreements over tariffs, trade negotiations and Russian oil purchases.
The discussions with Jaishankar are expected to cover a broad range of issues, from strategic cooperation and critical minerals to global conflicts and energy security. The visit to Reliance Industries’ Jamnagar refinery will also bring an economic and energy dimension to Rubio’s itinerary.
The outcome of the talks could help clarify the direction of bilateral engagement and identify areas where the two governments can make progress despite their differences. However, the future of trade negotiations and the handling of energy-related concerns remain important issues for both sides.

"Discussions covered key elements of a comprehensive peace framework, including long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic and prosperity plan, and a broader European security architecture designed to create lasting stability," the official said.
Release of 74-year-old American prisoner
Russia also released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American teacher from Michigan who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.
Hubbard was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison following a closed trial in 2024. Russian prosecutors alleged that he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Moscow launched its invasion in February 2022 and fought alongside Ukrainian forces until his capture two months later.
The Biden administration had designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained.
Witkoff thanked Putin for his release, saying, "Because of you, he's going home to his family." Putin confirmed that Hubbard was at St Petersburg's Pulkovo airport following his release.
Possible Putin-Trump meeting in China
Putin proposed meeting Trump in China, according to Russian state television, as quoted by Reuters. The Kremlin had previously raised the possibility of trilateral talks involving Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next month. No agreement on a meeting was immediately announced.
US-Russia economic cooperation and diesel exports
Putin also raised the possibility of restoring economic cooperation between Moscow and Washington. The discussions came as Russia prepared to dispatch its first diesel shipment to the United States on Thursday following an agreement with Trump.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the initial shipment would carry 40,000 metric tons of diesel, with further supplies expected.
"Additional shipments will follow, of course. There were agreements reached between the two leaders. We will meet the United States' needs, to the extent of our capabilities," Novak said, according to RIA.
Witkoff also thanked Putin for lifting restrictions on Russian diesel exports, while Putin said diesel prices had declined following the agreement.
Iran war and other discussions
The two sides also discussed Russia's willingness to help resolve the war in Iran, according to footage of the meeting reported by CNN.
Potential Russian fertiliser exports to the United States were among the other issues raised during the discussions, reflecting efforts to explore broader economic engagement alongside diplomatic negotiations.
Why the meeting matters
The meeting comes at a critical juncture in Washington's efforts to broker a settlement between Russia and Ukraine, with the two sides remaining deeply divided over territory and security guarantees.
Ukraine has insisted that any peace agreement must include credible guarantees against future Russian aggression and cannot require Kyiv to surrender territory.
Moscow, meanwhile, continues to demand control over the entire Donbas region, a reduction in Ukraine's military strength and assurances that Kyiv will never join NATO.
The talks also come amid growing strains between Washington and Kyiv following Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia under legislation aimed at restricting Moscow's war financing, alongside the agreement to import Russian diesel.
Ahead of the meeting, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned that Moscow would not make "political concessions" and said Russia did "not expect a miracle" from Witkoff's visit.
