Xi Jinping with Narendra Modi at the BRICS summit in New Delhi (Press Information Bureau, India)
Xi’s Delhi visit: China’s new tone, old assumptions about India
China’s president spoke of partnership in Delhi, but China’s longstanding doubts about India’s rise persist.
When China’s President Xi Jinping flew into (Opens in new window) New Delhi for the BRICS summit last month, it was his first visit to India in seven years. Meeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 12 September, Xi said the two countries should be “partners rather than rivals” (Opens in new window). Modi also spoke of improving ties. After years of tension along their Himalayan border, the language marked a welcome change.
But better relations do not necessarily mean a different view of each other. China and India have disputes over territory (Opens in new window), influence and international status. Some of those differences are rooted in how Chinese leaders have understood India’s place in Asia for more than a century.
The border dispute remains unresolved. A clash in the Galwan Valley in 2020 killed 20 Indian soldiers (Opens in new window) and, according to Beijing, four Chinese soldiers (Opens in new window). The two governments reached an agreement (Opens in new window) in 2024 that helped ease their military stand-off. Yet troops remain deployed (Opens in new window) along the disputed frontier, and negotiations over the boundary have made limited progress.
Bilateral trade reached a record $155.6 billion (Opens in new window) in 2025, according to Chinese customs figures. But India imported roughly $132 billion worth of Chinese goods in its 2025–26 financial year, leaving a trade deficit of more than $100 billion. New Delhi wants better access (Opens in new window) to the Chinese market and more dependable supply chains.
Their rivalry is not only about borders, trade or military power.
The gap in overall power is also large. In current US dollars, World Bank figures put China’s 2025 economy at about $19.5 trillion (Opens in new window), against nearly $4 trillion for India. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimates that China spent $336 billion (Opens in new window) on its military that year, compared with India’s $92.1 billion (Opens in new window). These differences help explain why Beijing may not see New Delhi as an equal strategic competitor. But they are not the whole explanation.
In a 2024 study (Opens in new window) called “Why Is China Dismissive of India’s Great Power Ambitions?,” in the Journal of Asian and African Studies, political scientist Raj Verma argued that China’s view of India has also been shaped by history and cognitive biases. Chinese intellectuals in the late 19th and early 20th centuries often treated British-ruled India as a warning of what might happen to their own country. They described India as a wang guo, or “lost country”. China faced foreign domination and unequal treaties but was never formally ruled as a single colony in the way India was under Britain.
Verma cites an earlier scholar’s account of Mao Zedong describing India in a 1970s poem as a cow, and a Peking University annotation of the poem that says the cow has “no particular talents” and that its ambitions are futile. He recounts the 1972 conversation with Henry Kissinger when Premier Zhou Enlai reportedly dismissed India’s prospects as “a bottomless hole (Opens in new window)”, and that earlier the writer Lu Xun had described Indians as “inferior slaves”. These remarks were not neutral descriptions of India. They reflected attitudes shaped by empire, nationalism and China’s own struggle for political survival.
Verma also argues that China’s revolutionary leaders were sceptical of India’s largely nonviolent independence movement. They had fought Japanese imperialism and a civil war, and often associated armed revolution with national strength. But India’s struggle also included armed resistance, a history that such judgements overlooked. Nor can remarks from earlier generations establish what Xi or today’s Chinese public thinks.
The BRICS declaration reiterated China’s support for India’s aspiration to play a greater role at the United Nations, including in the Security Council (Press Information Bureau, India)
Still, the attitudes are relevant because they predate the present economic gap. As Verma notes, the two economies were relatively close in size in 1978: around $150 billion for China and $137 billion for India. China’s dismissive image of India was already established.
Manjeet S. Pardesi reached a related conclusion in a 2021 study called (Opens in new window) “Explaining the asymmetry in the Sino-Indian Strategic Rivalry” in the Australian Journal of International Affairs. He described India as a “lesser” rival in Chinese strategic thinking, but one capable of obstructing Beijing’s wider ambitions in Asia. India therefore matters to China even when Beijing does not regard it as a peer. For New Delhi, China is a central security concern. Beijing, meanwhile, is more focused on its rivalry with the United States.
A third study offers a more optimistic reading. Writing in International Affairs in 2017, Xiaoyu Pu called China’s response to India’s rise “ambivalent accommodation” (Opens in new window). Beijing could welcome India as a partner among developing countries while hesitating to accept some of its great-power claims. Recognition, in this account, can change with political interests and the state of bilateral relations.
The September summit offers a test of that argument. Xi called for a more rational strategic perception of India. The BRICS declaration also reiterated (Opens in new window) China’s support for India’s aspiration to play a greater role at the United Nations, including in the Security Council. That language is not new, and it falls short of an explicit endorsement of a permanent Indian seat.
Now the question is whether India and China can move beyond the old assumptions that have shaped how they see each other. Their rivalry is not only about borders, trade or military power. History, national pride and long-held perceptions have also played a part. Better trade and more meetings between leaders may improve relations, but they will not necessarily change these views overnight.

India’s semiconductor ambitions are increasingly drawing in global materials suppliers, not just chip designers and fabricators. In a move that underlines that shift, Sumitomo Chemical has signed a memorandum of understanding with Tata Electronics to examine a possible collaboration in semiconductor fabrication and the supporting supply chain, according to specchemonline.com.
The agreement is significant because semiconductor manufacturing depends on a tightly controlled ecosystem of chemicals, photoresists and high-purity inputs. Any serious effort to localise chip production in India will need those upstream materials to be available reliably, at scale and with consistent quality. That is the business opportunity Sumitomo Chemical appears to be targeting through the Tata partnership.
What the agreement is meant to cover
The MoU does not amount to a final investment decision, but it signals intent. For Tata Electronics, which is building its semiconductor ambitions in India, a dependable materials partner could be as important as equipment, talent and policy support. For Sumitomo Chemical, the arrangement offers a way to align with a customer base that may grow as India pushes harder into advanced electronics manufacturing.
Why materials matter more than ever
That is why localisation efforts are increasingly extending beyond assembly and packaging. Countries seeking to build semiconductor resilience are now looking at the full stack, including the chemicals that enable chipmaking in the first place. A domestic or regional supply base can reduce logistics risk, shorten lead times and improve control over quality assurance.
Sumitomo Chemical is betting on semiconductor growthAsia Union Electronic Chemical, which operates facilities in Taiwan and Nevada. The company has also started work at advanced high-purity chemical centres in Japan and South Korea, where it is developing new processes and recycling technologies.
That sequence of investments suggests a broader strategy: deepen presence in major semiconductor geographies while improving supply resilience and technical capabilities. The India move fits that pattern, especially as chip manufacturing becomes more geographically diversified in response to geopolitical and supply chain concerns.India’s chip ecosystem is attracting upstream playerssemiconductors. The country’s appeal is no longer limited to final-stage electronics assembly. Global suppliers are beginning to evaluate whether India can support the specialised materials and process infrastructure needed for chip fabrication.
That shift matters because semiconductor projects are rarely built in isolation. A viable ecosystem requires chemical suppliers, gas suppliers, wafer handling, cleanroom services, logistics providers and a skilled technical workforce. The presence of a company such as Sumitomo Chemical would be a signal that India is moving closer to that broader industrial base.Regional competition is also intensifyingNissan Chemical, has separately set up a wholly owned subsidiary in Zhangjiagang in Jiangsu province, China. That unit will manufacture anti-reflective coatings used in photoresists and multilayer semiconductor materials.

A faster railway is not a freight corridor
Pakistan needs a freight system, not another list of projects
The Karachi–Rohri section of the Main Line-1 (ML-1) upgrade is estimated to cost about $2.5 billion. The Planning Ministry says the proposed modernisation would increase line capacity from 34 to 120 train pairs and raise freight speeds from around 30 to 80 km/h. These are projected improvements, not results yet achieved. Pakistan Railways issued an early market engagement notice for the project in September 2026. The question is what must change beyond the track itself for businesses to benefit from the investment.
The case for modernisation is clear: better track, signalling and operating capacity can improve the railway’s ability to carry freight. But infrastructure is only one part of the equation. Businesses also need dependable schedules, transparent charges, access to suitable rolling stock and timely information about when their cargo will arrive.
But a better railway does not automatically create a competitive freight system. PIDE’s transport and logistics research describes Pakistan’s freight movement as heavily dependent on roads, with rail accounting for a comparatively small share. This imbalance cannot be explained by track condition alone. The commercial appeal of rail also depends on reliability, total door-to-door cost, service frequency and how easily businesses can arrange shipments.
The evidence points to service, not only steel. PIDE’s transport and logistics research reports that freight forwarders have been reluctant to use Pakistan Railways because of unreliable services and limited access to relevant information. The research also discusses the open-access framework outlined by Pakistan Railways and the Infrastructure Project Development Facility in 2011, under which planned private-sector concessions were not activated. These findings point to a practical policy question: how can freight services become more predictable and accessible to commercial operators?
Pakistan has operated container trains between Karachi’s ports and inland freight terminals. A dedicated Karachi–Lahore freight train launched under a public-private partnership in December 2018, with an expected journey time of 48 hours. Officials presented the service as a way to reduce transport costs, but I could not establish whether these projected benefits were sustained in practice. That is precisely why route-level performance data matter. The government should publish comparable information on cost, transit time and reliability wherever commercially and operationally feasible.
CPEC 2.0 should connect assets into a working freight system and let route-level results guide the next round of public investment. Before committing to further investment, the government should be able to show what it costs, and how reliably, to move a defined container shipment from a production centre to the sea.
This matters to CPEC Phase II because regional connectivity requires more than physical links between locations. Pakistani producers must be able to move goods reliably towards ports and regional markets. A modernised railway that lacks predictable schedules, transparent handling charges and commercially workable access arrangements may fail to deliver its full freight potential. The route proposed below is a policy pilot; I do not claim that it is a formally designated CPEC route.
I propose a pilot Multimodal Freight Plan on one commercially viable route connecting Karachi’s ports with an inland freight terminal serving a major production cluster. Faisalabad is one candidate, but it should not be selected before comparison with alternatives such as Sialkot or Multan. Pakistan Railways, Karachi Port Trust, Port Qasim Authority and relevant terminal operators should supply available data on container volumes, costs, capacity and service performance. The route should be selected on evidence of demand and the feasibility of improving existing road–rail connections, not simply because infrastructure is already present. It would also distinguish operational failures from genuine infrastructure gaps.
For one defined container shipment type, the pilot would examine volumes and seasonality, road, rail and terminal costs, handling charges, timetables and frequency, capacity and its actual use, port access, and who sets tariffs at each handover. The assessment should compare like with like: the same shipment type, origin and destination, handling requirements and relevant service conditions.
The Ministry of Railways should coordinate the assessment with the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Karachi Port Trust, Port Qasim Authority, relevant dry-port operators and private freight forwarders, with each institution supplying data within its mandate. The first assessment can be done administratively from existing records. Wider private access to rail may need policy approval.
Not every constraint is the railway's, and not every answer is spending. Remedies might include better scheduling, clearer terminal terms, or access for the operators the 2011 policy anticipated. New capital works should follow only where a missing link is demonstrated. I would not start with a new logistics authority or subsidy.
The indicators would be: total cost of moving a defined container from origin to destination; transit time; rail's share of eligible containers; terminal and transfer dwell time; service frequency and on-time performance; capacity utilisation; private operators using the route; and bottlenecks found and resolved. I would avoid cost-per-tonne-kilometre comparisons unless distance, commodity and shipment size match. Data may be commercially sensitive, so results should be published in aggregate.
CPEC 2.0 should connect assets into a working freight system and let route-level results guide the next round of public investment. Before committing to further investment, the government should be able to show what it costs, and how reliably, to move a defined container shipment from a production centre to the sea.

articles.title: Recalibrating India–China Ties - Drishti IAS
articles.summary: Recalibrating India–China Ties  Drishti IAS
articles.full_text:
- 21 Oct 2026
- 28 min read
This editorial is based on "Time to engage smartly with China: Push premium Indian exports" published in The Economic Times on 19/10/2026. The article highlights that recalibrating economic ties with Beijing requires leveraging its offer to import premium Indian goods. Achieving balanced trade involves expanding PLIs for upstream components, dismantling entry barriers in IT and pharma, and securing critical rare earth supply chains.
The Union Minister of Commerce and Industry's recent call for a calibrated rebuilding of economic engagement with China underlines the need for a pragmatic dialogue that balances active trade stabilization with safeguards against structural vulnerabilities and strategic friction. New Delhi and Beijing are engaging in high-level talks to stabilize trade gains and build a shared vision for globalization, addressing both economic vulnerabilities and ongoing strategic friction. A pragmatic recalibration must reconcile competitive security needs with economic cooperation. As Dr. S. Jaishankar observes, "The key to a more settled Sino-Indian relationship is a greater acceptance by both countries of multipolarity and mutuality, building on a larger foundation of global rebalancing."
What are the Key Areas of Convergence between India and China?
- Border Stability, Confidence-Building and Strategic Communication: Both countries recognise the importance of peace and tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) for improving bilateral relations.  
  - At the 25th Special Representatives’ talks in August 2026, they agreed to two additional military meeting points and two additional border hotlines in the Eastern and Middle sectors. These confidence-building measures (CBMs) strengthen crisis communication and reduce the risk of miscalculation.
  - Dr. S Jaishankar’s formulation “manage China” offers a useful lens for this approach i.e., sustained diplomacy, military communication and negotiation remain essential even while the boundary question is unresolved.
- Economic Complementarities, and Supply-Chain Predictability: Large trade flows give both countries an economic stake in sustaining engagement, while India seeks reciprocity, diversified sourcing and meaningful market access.  
  - Official figures indicate bilateral merchandise trade of approximately USD 151 billion in FY2025–26, comprising Indian exports of USD 19.5 billion and imports of USD 131.6 billion.
  - Indian industrial sectors depend heavily on Chinese intermediate capital goods. GTRI estimates indicate that industrial products constitute approximately 98.5% of India’s imports from China. Separately, China accounts for around 43% of India’s electronics imports, 40% of machinery and computer imports, and 44% of organic-chemical imports, demonstrating significant sector-specific sourcing dependence.
- People-to-People Connectivity, Pilgrimage and Cultural Exchanges: Both sides support restoring civilian mobility, business travel and cultural interaction, creating visible public benefits from diplomatic normalisation.  
  - For example, Air India announced four weekly Delhi–Shanghai flights from February 2026, following bilateral agreements to restore air links.
  - The Sikkim government also confirmed that the first batch of Kailash Mansarovar Yatra 2026 returned through Nathu La on 1st July, 2026.
  - Such exchanges promote pilgrimage diplomacy, societal contact and tourism livelihoods, while providing practical opportunities to rebuild familiarity between the two populations.
- Transboundary River Dialogue, and Disaster Preparedness: Shared river systems create a practical need for technical communication, hydrological transparency and flood-risk reduction.  
  - During the August 2026 Special Representatives’ talks, both countries agreed to convene the next Expert-Level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers meeting and maintain communication on hydrological data sharing and renewal of relevant memoranda of understanding.
  - Providing real-time water flow, rainfall, and discharge metrics (for rivers like the Brahmaputra and Sutlej) during the critical monsoon window (May to October) assists Indian flood-management authorities in issuing early warnings across Assam and Arunachal Pradesh, balancing upstream dam construction with downstream disaster mitigation.
- Reformed Multilateralism, and Greater Global South Representation: India and China share an interest in international institutions reflecting the growing economic weight of emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs).  
  - The 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration, endorsed by both, supported stronger representation in the IMF and World Bank, inclusive leadership selection and meaningful quota realignment under the 17th General Review of Quotas.
  - Joint participation as important members of the BRICS+ bloc and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) aligns both nations in challenging Western-centric global financial and diplomatic dominance.
- Climate Equity, and Development-Sensitive Transitions: Both countries support climate action based on equity and Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC), including financial and technological support for developing countries.  
  - Cooperation also covers practical environmental priorities. China participated in the August 2026 BRICS environment meetings hosted by India, which advanced discussions on sustainable lifestyles, afforestation, forest-fire management, disaster resilience, circular economy and adaptation.
  - Both nations present a united front against unilateral Western environmental tariffs—such as the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)—demanding predictable climate finance transfers and equitable carbon space for industrializing economies.
- WTO-Centred Trade Governance, and MSME Internationalisation: Both countries support an effective rules-based multilateral trading system, which offers predictability for exporters and institutional avenues to address discriminatory restrictions.  
  - At the August 2026 BRICS Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Jaipur, attended by China’s trade representative, outcomes supported restoring a fully functioning, two-tier, binding WTO dispute-settlement system.  
    - Coordinating through the G33 coalition and Like-Minded Group (LMG) at the World Trade Organization (WTO) enables India and China to protect agrarian safety nets for hundreds of millions of smallholders.
  - Ministers also adopted credit-assessment principles for export-oriented MSMEs and agreed to study a BRICS invoice-discounting mechanism.
- Development Finance, Infrastructure Investment and South–South Cooperation: India and China cooperate as founding members of the New Development Bank (NDB), supporting additional financing channels for infrastructure and sustainable development.  
  - By 31st December 2025, the bank had approved USD 9.53 billion across 32 projects in India and USD 10 billion across 31 projects in China.
  - Coordinated participation under the G20 Common Framework for Debt Treatments prevents Western Paris Club creditors from dictating unilateral debt write-offs while ensuring that multilateral development banks (MDBs) de-risk infrastructure investments across the Global South.
What are the Key Areas of Divergence between India and China?
- Unresolved Line of Actual Control (LAC) and Militarization of Frontier Zones: Persistent disagreement over the demarcation of the 3,488-km Line of Actual Control (LAC)—compounded by China’s aggressive infrastructure building and deployment of troops across Western (Ladakh) and Eastern (Arunachal Pradesh) sectors—maintains a state of active military tension.  
  - Despite disengagement protocols across specific friction points following the 2020 Galwan Valley clash, China’s refusal to finalize a mutually agreed clarification of the LAC, coupled with illegal territorial claims over Arunachal Pradesh (which Beijing labels Zangnan), prevents normalization, forcing India to maintain permanent high-altitude deployments.
  - E.g., in April 2026, India rejected China’s assignment of new names to places in Indian territory. Such actions demonstrate how cartographic assertions and competing sovereignty narratives persist alongside diplomatic engagement.
- China–Pakistan Strategic Alignment, CPEC and India’s Security Concerns: China’s extensive defence partnership with Pakistan complicates India’s security calculations, while the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) raises sovereignty objections because it passes through Pakistan-occupied Indian territory.  
  - SIPRI’s 2026 assessment reports that China supplied 80% of Pakistan’s major-arms imports during 2021–25, illustrating the depth of this military relationship.  
    - Meanwhile, Beijing and Islamabad agreed in May 2026 to accelerate CPEC 2.0. Strategically, this reinforces India’s concern about a two-front security challenge.
  - Jaishankar’s insistence that connectivity requires “credible assurances that projects are not used to exert influence” captures the broader strategic sensitivity surrounding infrastructure corridors.
- Severe Structural Trade Deficit and Asymmetric Market Barriers: Economic commerce between the two Asian giants remains starkly unequal, driving India’s bilateral trade deficit to a historic $112.16 billion in FY 2025–26 (with imports scaling to $131.63 billion against Indian exports of just $19.47 billion).  
  - Chinese non-tariff trade barriers, stringent local registration norms, and state-subsidized dumping severely restrict Indian market access for IT services, generic pharmaceuticals, and agricultural commodities, reducing India to a primary raw-material exporter while creating dangerous supply-chain dependencies in critical sectors like Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) and solar wafers.

The growth forecast of Indian economy has been raised to 7.1% for 2026-27 from 6.7% projected in August but mounting inflationary pressures pose risks to the outlook, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said in the minutes of the central bank’s latest policy meeting.
"Amidst the turbulent global backdrop, the Indian economy has shown remarkable resilience. Growth for the full year 2026-27 is now projected at 7.1 per cent, 40 bps higher than the projection of 6.7 per cent in August. Inflationary pressures are, however, building up," said Malhotra.
The Reserve Bank on Wednesday released the minutes of the meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) held from October 5-7.
Along with the governor, the other five MPC members voted to raise the repo rate by 25 bps to 5.5 per cent.
The rate was hiked after a gap of nearly four years. The country's growth has held up better than expected, inflation risks are building again and the global interest-rate environment is making it harder for India to maintain a wide policy gap. The rate hike marks the first increase since February 2023, when it stood at 6.6%, and a reversal from the RBI’s rate-cut cycle, with the central bank now having greater confidence that the economy can absorb some monetary tightening without a significant hit to growth.
The governor noted that there are increasing signs of generalisation of inflation as 37 per cent of the commodities in the CPI basket had inflation above 4 per cent in August -- it was merely 20 per cent in March, said the minutes of the MPC meeting released on Wednesday.

articles.summary: ‘Demands comprehensive federal response’: 105 US lawmakers urge FBI to probe Hindu temple shooting plot a  The Times of IndiaProbe Hindu temple attack as hate crime, US lawmakers tell FBI chief Kash Patel  RediffOver 100 US lawmakers seek hate crime probe into Illinois temple attack  India TodayMEA calls on U.S. to ensure safety, security of Indians after foiled Illinois temple attack  The HinduNot ‘widespread’: Marco Rubio dismisses anti-India sentiment i...
articles.full_text:
A group of 105 US lawmakers has urged the FBI to investigate an alleged shooting plot at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, as a potential federal hate crime, citing concerns about anti-Indian, anti-Hindu and broader anti-South Asian hostility.
Led by Indian American Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, wrote to FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday, asking for an update on the investigation into the alleged plot at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) temple and the bureau’s efforts to address credible threats against South Asian communities.
Krishnamoorthi and his family were worshipping at the temple when the alleged incident occurred on October 11.
“The alleged combination of targeted racial hatred, a religious setting, and preparations for mass violence demands a comprehensive federal response,” the lawmakers wrote.
The group included the entire Illinois House Democratic delegation, every Indian American member of Congress, and Senators Dick Durbin, Tammy Duckworth, Andy Kim and Chris Van Hollen.
Alexandros Paporakis, 19, was arrested on October 11 in connection with the alleged plot. According to prosecutors, he attempted to shoot a man outside the temple, but his rifle jammed. He fled the scene and later communicated plans to return, prompting a co-worker to alert police, who arrested him that day.
Prosecutors allege that Paporakis, who identified himself as a neo-Nazi, wrote an eight-page white supremacist manifesto describing violence against people of Indian descent at a Hindu place of worship. Investigators recovered a rifle, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, body armour and white supremacist imagery, as per the press release.
The letter asks whether the FBI is examining potential racial, ethnic and religious bias in the case and whether online platforms or other individuals may have helped facilitate the alleged plot. The lawmakers also want to know whether the bureau is coordinating with the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division and the relevant US Attorney’s Office.
The request comes amid concerns about online hate targeting South Asians in the US. The lawmakers cited a September 2026 report that identified more than 542,000 anti-South Asian hateful posts on X between January 2025 and June 2026. The monthly volume reportedly rose by about 240% between January 2024 and June 2026.
They also cited a Carnegie Endowment survey in which 48% of Indian American respondents said they had encountered racist posts targeting their community very or somewhat often since the start of 2025. One in four respondents reported being called a slur.
The letter criticised messages posted by Trump administration agencies that the lawmakers said risk reinforcing racial and religious stereotypes. Examples included a Department of Homeland Security post targeting a Sikh man with a remark about driving and a Department of Education post declaring “Make College Football Great Again” after a Texas Republican complained about South Asians attending a University of Texas football game.
The lawmakers argued that political debates over immigration and public safety should not lead to collective suspicion of Indian, Sikh, Hindu or other South Asian communities.
They have asked the FBI to clarify how it distinguishes protected speech, including offensive expression, from credible threats that warrant investigation. They also want details of how actionable intelligence is shared with local law enforcement and potentially targeted places of worship.
Other questions concern whether the bureau has sufficient personnel, language expertise and analytical resources to assess threats involving anti-Indian, anti-Hindu and broader anti-South Asian bias.
The lawmakers requested a written response by October 29, to the extent permitted by the ongoing investigation. They urged the bureau to examine all relevant evidence, pursue applicable offences and explain what steps are being taken to protect affected communities.

articles.title: Italy’s Meloni toughens protest laws: Teen detentions, parental liability, 5-year jail term - The Times of India
articles.summary: Italy’s Meloni toughens protest laws: Teen detentions, parental liability, 5-year jail term  The Times of IndiaWhat are Italy’s new measures against violent protests?  Al JazeeraIndia asks citizens in Italy, Albania to exercise caution amid unrest  Scroll.inItaly to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and looting  The GuardianVandalism is criminality: Meloni makes parents liable for children's vandalism  India Today
articles.full_text:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government has approved tougher security measures targeting protest-related violence, including prison terms of up to five years, fines of up to €20,000 and financial liability for parents whose children engage in vandalism or looting.
The measures, which took effect immediately on Tuesday, follow weekend unrest in northern Italian cities, including Milan, where groups of mainly young people smashed windows, looted shops and attacked police.
Under the new rules, people participating in groups of at least five who endanger public safety during demonstrations can face up to five years in prison and a maximum fine of €20,000 ($22,460). Penalties can increase if protesters conceal their faces or injure others.
Authorities can also order compensation for damage caused during unrest, with parents held financially liable when their minor children are responsible.
The decree further allows police to detain young people aged 14 to 17, even if they have not committed a crime, if there is evidence they pose a danger. Previously, this power applied only to adults.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalising and stealing. 
Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media while announcing the measures.
The government has also announced the deployment of 500 army troops alongside police in Milan until the end of 2026. The troops will help secure key sites, monitor sensitive locations and strengthen surveillance, the defence ministry said.
 Meloni faces pressure over unrest and rising prices
The security crackdown comes as Meloni's government faces protests on multiple fronts. In southern Italy, truck drivers angered by rising diesel prices and the cost of living have staged roadblocks, disrupting supply chains. Some pasta manufacturers have halted production, while agricultural groups have warned that fruit and vegetables could go to waste.
The government has promised additional aid for road hauliers following talks with industry representatives.
Meloni, who has introduced a series of security measures since taking office in 2022, has faced criticism from opponents who argue that tougher penalties do little to address the underlying causes of crime and disorder. Government data shows Italy's prison population has risen by more than 17% over four years, an increase of nearly 10,000 people.
Acknowledging the economic difficulties facing households, Meloni said hardship could not justify violence.
“We know what it means to look for a job, to earn an insufficient wage, and to see no prospects for the future ... but hardship must never be used as an excuse for violence,” she said on Tuesday.
With national elections due in 2027, protests over both public order and the rising cost of living present a challenge for the government.

articles.title: ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’: What does this viral message from French protests mean - The Times of India
articles.summary: ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’: What does this viral message from French protests mean  The Times of IndiaWhy are French protesters chanting ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’?  Al JazeeraStudent Protesters in France Have a Strange New Slogan. What Does It Mean?  The New York Times"Bismillah, C'est Les Tenebres": What Slogan Dominating France Protests Means  NDTVFrench students turn awkward slogan into protest rallying cry | Daily Sabah  Daily Saba...
articles.full_text:
France’s high school protests have given rise to a string of slogans, but one cryptic phrase has emerged as an unlikely rallying cry. “Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres”, also repeated by climate activist Greta Thunberg, has spread from placards outside blockaded schools to viral videos.
The phrase originated in a Snapchat message that students suspect was sent by an undercover police officer.
Protesters have turned it into a running joke, using it to mock what they believe was an attempt by police to infiltrate their private protest groups. The slogan has since spread beyond France, appearing at demonstrations in Belgium and Italy.
Students say it makes fun of someone attempting, and failing, to sound like a teenager, as per Euro News. However, it is seen as a shorthand for a generational divide, as per The New York Times.
What does ‘bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’ mean?
“Bismillah” is Arabic for “in the name of God” and is traditionally said before beginning a task. In everyday French slang, it can also mean something like “let’s go”.
“C’est les ténèbres” translates as “it’s the darkness”. Young people use the expression as slang for a situation that is grim or catastrophic.
Together, the words roughly mean “In the name of God, it’s the darkness”. Students have turned the phrase into a joke about what they see as an attempt by suspected undercover officers to imitate youth slang while trying to gather information about protests
The phrase came from a screenshot of a Snapchat conversation that began circulating in early October, when students were using the platform to organise school blockades.
In the message, a user named “Mamadou” asks to join a group, writing: “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?"
However, neither the French police nor the interior ministry has commented on the screenshots, and the identities of the accounts have not been independently verified.
Some social media users claimed to have traced the accounts to locations near police stations, but those claims remain unverified.
Why are French students protesting?
The movement began in Créteil, south-east of Paris, on September 18 and quickly spread across France.
Students have protested against long school days, overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating school buildings and teacher absences. Many argue that these problems disproportionately affect working-class suburbs and minority communities.
Around 400 schools were closed by blockades on October 2 alone.
The student demonstrations later fed into nationwide cost-of-living protests on October 17, which ended in rioting and looting.

LONDON: Two British Indian Telugu Hindu men were assaulted during a Dussehra and Bathukamma celebration in the town of Ossett, West Yorkshire, last Saturday night in what police believe was a racially aggravated attack. The assaults happened on Oct 17 outside Ossett Town Hall, which was hosting the celebration. The event was organised by local Telugu Hindu community groups.
Earlier in the evening a group of around 25 local white youths, mostly male, were cycling around on e-bikes asking organisers what was going on in the town hall and who was inside. Some of them tried to force their way in, but security did not allow it.
One of the victims, a 51-year-old British Indian man from the Hyderabad region, left the event at around 9pm and walked to his car with a friend. As they did so, they encountered a group of eight to 10 youths, some in black balaclavas.
“One of them approached us and started asking us why we were here, what we were doing and looked aggressive,” he told TOI. “He circled around us and used filthy language. We didn’t respond. We didn’t feel it was safe to go further and started to go back to town hall and then he hit both of us. He hit me hard and pushed me to the ground on my face and left me bleeding. 
I stood up and then he punched me in my left eye … My friend was left with a head injury and his hand was bleeding.”
There have been no arrests yet. Inspector Andrew Dickinson said: “We recognise the distress thishas caused to the wider Hindu community. We are treating these assaults seriously and are working to ensure those responsible are held accountable.”

In an emotional message to supporters, Dipke urged them to spend time with their families during the festive period, while remembering Das and Ranka, who have been in jail since October 13 and could not be with their loved ones. He said the families of those involved in the movement were also bearing the consequences of their decision to protest.
"For a few days, spend time with your families. Be there with your families, be there with your loved ones," he said, adding, "Please remember Sourav and Ashu when you are with your families, because they both can't be with their families. So they are our family."
Referring to those drawing parallels with unrest abroad, Dipke said the CJP leaders had not resorted to violence despite being jailed. Instead, they had accepted their imprisonment with a smile, he said.
"Have some shame and see what is happening in India. In India, Sourav Das and Ashutosh went to jail happily. They did not do what is happening in France," he said.
The CJP and its supporters have been protesting against the SIR of electoral rolls and demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Das and Ranka were arrested after CJP activists entered Jantar Mantar on October 13, a day after it was removed from the list of designated protest sites. The two were initially remanded to judicial custody for five days, which was extended by two more days on October 19.
"I am telling you, when Sourav and Ashutosh will come out, they will again come out of jail with the same smile. They will come out of jail and they will again walk on the path of Mahatma Gandhi, of peace and non-violence," Dipke said.
He also cautioned supporters against turning to hatred due to the treatment meted out to the two leaders, saying the movement's commitment to compassion was its greatest strength.
"We are fighting against hatred; we are fighting against the people who have nothing but hatred in their mind. But we also have to ensure that hatred does not come inside us," he said.
"We don't have to become what we hate," he stressed, accusing those opposing the movement of trying to provoke its members into abandoning their peaceful approach.
The CJP founder acknowledged that the past several days had been difficult for volunteers, some of whom he said had faced detention and alleged beatings during the protests.
However, he said their families were experiencing an even greater strain because they had not chosen to be part of the struggle.
"The fight that we are putting up was our decision. But the consequences of that are also coming on our families," he said, asking supporters to stay close to their loved ones.
Dipke said he had spoken to the families of both jailed leaders and drawn strength from their resolve. He said Das's mother had reassured him that her son was a fighter and urged him to tell others to take care of themselves.
Ranka, meanwhile, could not attend a funeral in his family after a relative died while he was in jail, Dipke said. Despite the circumstances, he said, Ranka's family had also urged him not to worry about the two leaders.
"The people who should have been weak, they are not weak. In fact, they are the ones who are giving me the strength," he said.
Dipke credited Das and Ranka with playing a major role in taking the movement forward, saying he had largely followed their instructions while organising the protests.
He recalled how Das had once been mocked for being too privileged or soft to withstand jail, including for drinking cold coffee during protests. Das had nevertheless spent several days in custody and appeared in court smiling, Dipke said.
He also spoke emotionally about his bond with the two, describing them as his brothers and saying he continued to open a WhatsApp group where they used to share memes simply to feel that they were still part of it.
"Our emotions are not our weakness. They are our strength," he said, adding that the movement would continue with love, compassion and the values of Gandhi and B R Ambedkar.
Dipke said the movement would not retreat because of the arrests, while urging supporters to take care of themselves and their families.
"We will not back down. It is not that if Sourav and Ashu go to jail, we will be scared," he said.

articles.title: 'India is their main target': RSS Chief Mohan Bhagwat warns of foreign forces trying to dismantle country, says regime change won't help - News24Online

articles.full_text:
Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat on Tuesday warned that attempts to weaken India would not succeed, arguing that political changes alone cannot resolve the country’s challenges. Speaking at the organisation’s Vijayadashami Utsav in Nagpur, he urged people to remain alert to external influences and find solutions through society rather than street protests.
His remarks came amid demonstrations over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and a political dispute over the demand for regime change.
Bhagwat flags threats to India’s stability
Bhagwat said India had become a target because of its progress and decisive policy decisions over recent decades. He argued that some forces wanted to disrupt the country’s development and weaken both India and the RSS.
‘This has never happened before and will not happen again,’ he said, rejecting the idea that changing the government would automatically transform the country’s circumstances.
He also cautioned against politically motivated demonstrations, saying such activities could lead to tension, disorder and disruptions to public life. According to him, lasting solutions must emerge from within society.
‘Storm coming from the West’
The RSS chief warned of international forces seeking to divert India from its development goals. Referring to what he described as a ‘storm coming in from the West’, he alleged that some powers opposed India’s culture, systems and security.
He cited France, Nepal and Bangladesh while discussing alleged foreign interference and attempts to bring about regime changes. Bhagwat also criticised sections of Indian society whom he accused of supporting such interests.
Political row over regime change
His comments followed senior Supreme Court lawyer Prashant Bhushan’s recent remarks on protests over alleged SIR irregularities. Bhushan said the movement had become ‘really a fight for regime change’, adding that continued brutality could eventually lead to such a change.
The BJP criticised his statement. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh accused unnamed groups of using young people to encourage political unrest, while party spokesperson CR Kesavan described the protests as a ‘smokescreen’ for an alleged opposition effort to bring down the government.
Development must protect nature
Bhagwat also called for a development model that respects ecology, ethics and India’s religious, linguistic and food diversity. Citing floods in Nepal and the Kolkata stampede deaths, he stressed the need to distinguish natural disasters from human failures.
He warned that development across the Himalayan region, including India, Nepal and China, must not come at the cost of human lives. India, he said, should set an example by balancing progress with public safety and environmental protection.

articles.title: In absence of sovereign buyers, Indian chip firms find clients in Japan, EU - Livemint
articles.summary: In absence of sovereign buyers, Indian chip firms find clients in Japan, EU  Livemint
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI : India’s early movers in semiconductor engineering and design are chasing clients abroad as demand from within India remains tepid. At least three companies in the country’s semiconductor industry, including Tata Electronics, have identified global clients as key to generating commercial revenue starting this fiscal year.
On 16 December last year, homegrown electronics manufacturer Kaynes Technology India Limited’s wholly owned chipmaking subsidiary, Kaynes Semicon Private Limited, announced a deal with Japan-based investment firm Mitsui & Co, receiving regulatory clearance on 9 March. The deal, Mitsui said in a press statement then, will “support sales of products manufactured by Kaynes”.
Later, on 17 September, Tata Electronics signed a partnership with Nexperia, a global manufacturer of automotive semiconductors. Nexperia, Tata Electronics said in a press release, will be a key customer for its outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) plant in Jagiroad, Assam.
For India’s key semiconductor firms, global clients are among the most immediate sources of commercial demand. CG Semi, a joint-venture subsidiary of CG Power and Industrial Solutions Ltd, announced on 1 July that it had begun commercial chip supplies to Japan’s Renesas Electronics Corp. in June this year. Renesas, to be sure, is also a captive client, as it holds a 6.8% stake in CG Semi.
Industry stakeholders and companies that Mint spoke with said that the rising revenue scope from global chip clients is the natural course of action, as sovereign demand from within India is yet to pick up pace. A senior executive close to developments at Tata Semiconductor Assembly and Test (TSAT) Private Limited, who requested anonymity, said “it will take some time for India to build scale as a semiconductor client base.”
A demand gap
“Most users of chips, such as power, automotive, aviation and other sectors, have set vendors with long-term contracts around the world. These contracts aren’t easy to break just because there’s a new facility somewhere. Sovereign demand from within India, at any rate, was meant to be sourced through government procurement deals—which are either too small and at early pilot stages, or are too few to meaningfully count for now,” the executive said.
A senior executive close to developments at Kaynes Semicon, said global clients are important because revenue does not depend on whether a customer is Indian or foreign.
“There are many global compound semiconductor makers for which we will be offering packaging services. But, the global semiconductor supply chain does not work in silos—they work as a chain. Often, a European fabless chipmaker would be serving Indian industrial clients. It’s a circular economy, and that is why it is important for us to have ample global firms to cater to.”
Global value chains
The Centre, however, has not outlined a specific roadmap for providing anchor-client opportunities to companies incentivized under the India Semiconductor Mission, the incentive scheme of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) that supported each of the three companies cited above.
On 23 August, MeitY secretary S. Krishnan told Mint that the ministry would back Indian chip companies in becoming globally successful, rather than limiting their focus to the domestic market.
“We are not a closed economy. We are not going to say you should use only chips made here. Anything that we make should be part of a global value chain—if you’re not able to produce for the export market, then you’re not being fair to your own country. Whatever we support will have to be globally competitive. They may need some support to reach scale before they become globally competitive—that we can support, but in the long term, they should be able to sell in the global market competitively,” Krishnan said.
Since 2021, New Delhi has announced incentives worth ₹2.04 trillion ($21.5 billion) to encourage the establishment of one contractual pure-play chip fabrication plant, two compound semiconductor fabs and nine chip testing and assembly facilities. Of these, CG Semi and Kaynes have begun early-stage commercial production at their respective OSAT facilities in Sanand, Gujarat. TSAT, Mint reported on 5 October, expects its chip testing facility to begin commercial production before December.
The course has thus shifted the narrative from sovereign clients in semiconductors, to global ones. To keep pace, even startups believe that global clients will be key. One such is Peak XV-backed Mindgrove Technologies, which expects to generate its first operating revenue this fiscal. Shashwath TR, cofounder and chief executive, told Mint last month that it “is not really differentiating between international and Indian clients,” as it seeks to sell Indian chip designs to industrial clients worldwide.

articles.title: Pakistan-United States relations: Why Trump is sending “Thank You Pakistan” messages to Islamabad? - Prothom Alo English
articles.summary: Pakistan-United States relations: Why Trump is sending “Thank You Pakistan” messages to Islamabad?  Prothom Alo English
articles.full_text:
Opinion
Pakistan-United States relations: Why Trump is sending “Thank You Pakistan” messages to Islamabad
When the slogan “Thank You Pakistan” rang out in the Iranian parliament, most Pakistanis were delighted. But after trade with Iran was halted, Donald Trump began sending “Thank You Pakistan” messages to Islamabad. Public discontent in Pakistan is evident as these tactically worded expressions of gratitude have sparked fresh tensions with its neighbour. Hamid Mir has written about the matter.
In June 2025, "Thank You Pakistan" slogans rang out in the Iranian Parliament. The reason was obvious: Pakistan had not only condemned Israeli aggression against Iran but also supported it at every international forum. Pakistan again played a key role in brokering a ceasefire between Iran and the United States in April 2026, and once more several Iranian TV channels aired Persian songs saying "Thank You Pakistan." Iranians waved Pakistani flags at anti-US rallies in Tehran. The two countries opened several border crossings to promote trade, but this love affair came to an end on 17 October 2026.
The newspapers of October 18 carried the troubling report that Pakistan had temporarily closed its border crossings with Iran, including Gabd-Rimdan. Gabd lies in Pakistani Balochistan and Rimdan in Iranian Balochistan, and the crossing is just 87 kilometers from Gwadar Port. A few months ago, when tensions between Iran and the United States disrupted trade through the Strait of Hormuz, traffic at Gwadar suddenly increased.
As Gwadar grew in importance, trade between Pakistan and Iran also began through Gabd and Rimdan. Iranian companies and traders started ordering goods to Gwadar, and from there the cargo reached Iran in two hours. The crossing was also busier because it was safer than the Taftan-Zahedan border.
Now a spokesperson for the Balochistan government says the crossing was closed because of the poor law and order situation and smuggling. Iran's Foreign Ministry gave a cautious statement, saying the border has been closed temporarily for "technical reasons." Reports indicate that the situation is the same at Taftan-Zahedan, and thousands of containers are stuck at both crossings. Trade routes between Pakistan and India, and between Pakistan and Afghanistan, were already closed. With Iran's routes now shut as well, Gwadar Port will suffer the most. The closure may also raise liquefied gas prices in Pakistan, as more than 4,000 tonnes of LPG were entering the country daily through Gabd-Rimdan.
Gwadar is only 400 kilometers from the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world''s oil trade passes. Tensions over Hormuz temporarily increased Gwadar''s importance, but sadly the Pakistani government seems to be struggling to sustain it. The port is needed not only by Iran but also by many countries of South Asia, Central Asia, and West Asia. In 2019, Saudi Arabia's Aramco expressed interest in building a ten-billion-dollar oil refinery here. The Saudi company wanted China to join the project as a partner, but the talks did not progress. The Chinese have been under attack in Balochistan since 2013, and Pakistan accuses India and Afghanistan of cross-border terrorism there. Pakistan shares more than 2600 kilometers border with Afghanistan and 900 kilometers border with Iran.
The Saudis wanted Chinese partnership in Gwadar to address security concerns, but China declined for several reasons, not least that it never wanted to offend Iran. Since the Iran-America war the refinery project has been stalled, and after the recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia its prospects have diminished further. Gwadar is only 87 kilometers from Iran, and Pakistan is part of a joint defense alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkey. Iranian-backed Houthis have targeted Aramco in Saudi Arabia many times. They could do the same in Pakistan.
Ever since work began on Gwadar Port under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), terrorism in Balochistan has increased. Not just one enemy country is behind it; some friendly Gulf countries also have a hand, as they fear Gwadar's development will affect their own ports. To put an end to these conspiracies, Pakistan some time ago offered the United States the chance to develop Pasni Port, only one hundred kilometers from Gwadar. But US authorities seem more interested in the mineral wealth of Balochistan than in developing Pasni. The Makran coast has not only Gwadar and Pasni but also the ports of Jiwani, Ormara, and Sonmiani. Balochistan has both coastline and resources, yet because of bad governance and terrorism, no improvement in its situation is visible.
I still remember that when Dr. Shireen Mazari was head of the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad, President General Pervez Musharraf told us there that he was handing over the blue waters of Gwadar to China, and that it would now be for China and India to deal with each other. Former Foreign Minister Agha Shahi was not at all pleased to hear this. Puffing vigorously on his pipe, he told me that China was certainly our friend, but if Gwadar Port were handed over without an effective strategy, Balochistan would become a center of international conspiracies.
One great tragedy of Pakistan is that our rulers have no knowledge of the history of its provinces and important regions. History is deeply connected with geography, and if lessons are not learned from history, geography changes. Our rulers must read the history of Gwadar and the Makran coast. Sahil-e-Makran, by Professor Dr. Hameed Baloch of Lasbela University, Uthal, Balochistan, should be read by every policymaker and every student of history in Pakistan. This two-volume work is a treasure not only of knowledge but also of historical documents, which show that British forces used small airfields along the Makran coast to attack Japanese forces.
Many years ago, when I first went to Gwadar, the elders showed me their old passports issued by the Sultanate of Oman. Gwadar remained part of Oman until 1958, when, on 6 September, a weak political government under Malik Feroz Khan Noon paid three million British pounds to bring it into Pakistan. The Khan of Kalat, Nasir Khan I, had given Gwadar in 1783 to a rebel prince of Muscat, and later tried to take it back without success. The Omani government earned considerable profit from the taxes levied at Gwadar Port. The Khan of Kalat then reduced taxes at the ports of Pasni and Jiwani, which diminished Gwadar's importance, after which the British government began to consider handing Gwadar over to Kalat. Some British oil companies, unhappy with the rulers of Oman, also played an important role in this.
Dr. Hameed Baloch also writes that, after the creation of Pakistan, All India Radio one day broadcast a false report that the Khan of Kalat had decided to merge his state with India. The Khan, Ahmad Yar Khan, immediately sent a telegram to Viceroy Lord Mountbatten asking that the report be denied. Reacting to this false news, he decided to accede to Pakistan in March 1948, and with the accession of Kalat, Pasni and Jiwani also came under Pakistan's control. In 1954, the US Geological Survey declared Gwadar a great port of the future.
The Omani government wanted to hand Gwadar over to India, but India was then more interested in Goa. India took Goa by military action, while Pakistan acquired Gwadar from Oman through negotiation. The political government that brought Gwadar into Pakistan was removed within weeks, when General Ayub Khan imposed martial law in October 1958. Gwadar was incorporated into Pakistan, but the fortunes of Gwadar and Balochistan have not changed to this day. A few days ago the establishment imposed Governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to fight terrorism, yet the situation in Balochistan is worse than in KP.
The sudden decision to close the Gabd-Rimdan crossing has caused turmoil and uproar not only in Gwadar but all over Balochistan. The cries of Baloch businessmen have reached me through officials of the Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry, but perhaps they have not reached the rulers in Islamabad. There is an impression that Pakistan closed its trade routes with Iran under American pressure. This closure may help the US, but it is definitely hurting Pakistan.
Remember: until there is stability on the Makran coast, Balochistan will not be stable, and if Balochistan is not stable, Pakistan cannot move forward. Pakistan should not act like a proxy of the US, nor become a source of pleasure for Israel. Tension between Pakistan and Iran will please Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu. When "Thank You Pakistan" slogans were raised in the Iranian Parliament, the majority of Pakistanis were very happy.
After the closure of trade with Iran, Donald Trump is sending "Thank You Pakistan" messages to Islamabad. We cannot hear this mischievous thank-you, but we can see the unhappiness in Pakistan over a new tension with another neighbor. Pakistanis were happy to mediate between Iran and US but they will not accept collaboration with US against Iran. I hope that recent visit of Pakistani head of the Armed Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir to Iran will remove misunderstandings between the countries and Pakistan will restrict only to a mediator.
*Hamid Mir is a Pakistani journalist.
#The opinions expressed here are the author's own.

A California-based tech firm, Cloudera, has reached a settlement of $2 million with the Department of Justice and the Department of Labor on allegations that the company discriminated against qualified US workers when it filed for Green Cards for its foreign workers. Additionally, the company will be banned from the Green Card process for two years. Cloudera's Green Card ban was announced earlier -- before the Donald Trump administration banned the Green Card process of eight major tech companies, including Microsoft and Adobe. Cloudera's case is different as there was a lawsuit filed against Cloudera in April this year.
There are no exceptions: Harmeet K Dhillon
“There are no exceptions: the Justice Department will hold accountable employers who discriminate against US workers,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “This substantial settlement, in partnership with DOL, sends a strong signal to employers that the federal government will work together to ensure employers treat US workers fairly.”
In April, DOJ filed a lawsuit alleging that Cloudera alleging that the company violated the Immigration and Nationality Act by discriminating against US workers "when recruiting and hiring for seven positions under the PERM process".
The Justice Department said that under the terms of the settlement,, Cloudera will establish a back-pay fund of $1.4 million to compensate qualified US workers who tried to apply for the jobs at issue but were not given fair consideration. Cloudera will also pay $600,000 in civil penalties to the United States.
"Cloudera will be subject to compliance obligations designed to ensure future adherence to federal labor and anti-discrimination laws. These measures include enhanced monitoring, revised PERM compliance procedures, and reporting requirements intended to prevent future violations," the department said.
The PERM (Program Electronic Review Management) process is the mandatory first step for US employers sponsoring a foreign national for an employment-based green card (typically EB-2 or EB-3). It is designed to prove to the US Department of Labor (DOL) that there are no qualified, willing, and available US workers for the job, and that hiring the foreign worker will not lower local wages. But Cloudera asked applicants to send their applications an email address that did not accept outside emails.
